British Columbians delivered a clear mandate for change, jobs, affordability and common sense. Voters rejected Premier Eby's attempt to make the election about Donald Trump instead of his government's dismal record. They want action on job losses, rising costs and the struggling economy. Lorne Doerkson's team will advance major projects, deliver tax relief and restore fiscal responsibility. Repealing DRIPA will provide investors greater certainty.
Congratulations locally to Lawrence Mok, Doug Morneau and Darryl Kropp.

Now, the Liberals must step up. British Columbians cannot afford more delays and empty promises. They must fast-track approvals, remove investment barriers and work together with a new B.C. Conservative government to fire up B.C.'s economy and get people back to work.
Mr. Speaker, last October 11, I organized a “Tribute to Men of Terrebonne” ceremony in honour of five outstanding men—
May I ask the hon. member to start again? There was too much noise in the chamber.
Mr. Speaker, last October 11, I organized a “Tribute to Men of Terrebonne” ceremony to honour five outstanding men for their amazing contributions to our community.

Today, I wish to honour Chadi Ayoub for his commitment to the arts and to promoting the region's culture; Éric Barrette, for his dedication to education, sports and the success of our youth; Gilles Bordonado, for his contribution to journalism, communications and our community's development; Raymond Paquin, for his incredible work to preserve our history and heritage; and Dr. Harry Max Prochette, for his devotion to the health and well-being of our citizens.

These five men remind us that commitment comes in many forms, but always targets the same goal: to improve the lives of others. To each of these gentlemen, I offer my gratitude for your dedication and your contributions to our community. You are the pride of Terrebonne.

Mr. Speaker, we have good news. This past Saturday, the people of British Columbia delivered a strong and historic message. For the first time in nearly 100 years, British Columbians elected a Conservative majority government.

The B.C. Conservatives secured a powerful mandate of over 60 seats, bringing an end to the nine years of the costly NDP government. From the Lower Mainland to the interior, from the Fraser Valley to communities large and small, British Columbians chose change. They chose a government committed to lowering costs, cutting red tape and putting hard-working families first.
I want to congratulate Premier-elect Lorne Doerkson, every Conservative candidate and every voter who refused to accept the status quo.

This was more than just an election victory. It was a powerful reminder that common-sense Conservative principles resonate with Canadians. The blue wave is strong, our movement is growing and this is just the beginning.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to honour the incredible life of Gord Hume, a Londoner who passed away recently at the age of 76.

Gord was born in Saskatoon. He came to London in 1980. He first worked in news media, but made his most lasting contributions to our community as a city councillor. He was elected in 1997, was on the council until 2010, and especially contributed, through the millennium committee formed in 1998, to the revitalization of the Covent Garden Market, to the revitalization of the Central Library and to what was then called the John Labatt Centre, but is now called the Canada Life Place. This is the home of the London Knights, which is a landmark in London, to say the least. Gord also worked as a novelist, producing a number of books, and wrote widely on municipal government.
This was a true Londoner. This was a great Canadian. Our city is less because of his passing. Our city was great because of Gord and people like him.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, demand is soaring. Le Journal de Québec reported that a charity called Le Marginal served 400 meals in a single evening. That is five times more than 10 years ago. However, it seems that the Prime Minister has learned nothing. He is still forecasting $730 billion of inflationary debt within five years, which will further fuel inflation.
Why are Canadians being asked to pay more for his debt than for the food they put on their tables?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the people of Quebec City who are watching us will realize that, sadly, the leader of the Conservative Party, who is the Leader of the Opposition, did two things when the House had the opportunity to vote on the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, a measure that helps 12 million Canadians, including many in Quebec City. One, he voted against the benefit. Two, he instructed his caucus to vote against it. The people of Quebec City will remember that.
On this side of the House, we will always be there to stand up for the people of Quebec City.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, all of these inflationary Liberal programs are not working for the 400 people who were in need of a hot meal.

It is not just the demand for hot meals that is skyrocketing. The Liberals' inflationary debt is too. According to a report by the Parliamentary Budget Officer, the Prime Minister is going to add $730 billion to our debt. That is going to drive up the cost of living. It is going to cost a family of four $6,000 in interest a year.
Why must Canadians feed the Liberal debt instead of feeding their families?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, after spending two decades in the House, the Conservative leader should know one thing: When it comes to helping Canadians, he should put politics aside and vote to help them. Twelve million Canadians will receive the Canada groceries and essentials benefit, which provides up to $1,891 for a family of four. That is money that is going into families' bank accounts to help them.
Will the Conservative leader stand up and say that he will now support our measures to help Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Liberal Prime Minister is out of touch, Canadians are out of money and the debt is out of control. More inflation is on the horizon as the Parliamentary Budget Officer calculated that the government is expected to add $730 billion to our national debt over the next five years. That is three-quarters of a trillion dollars more on the national credit card, working out to $40,000 in debt for every single Canadian. That is more handouts to corporate power brokers, more interest to bankers, and more food and housing inflation for Canadians.
How does he expect them to pay this bill?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will take no lessons from the Conservatives. Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have one of the most educated workforces in the world. We are able to build planes, build ships and build cars in this country. We have the critical minerals to power the economy of the 21st century. We have an abundance of energy and we are going to produce even more. We are the only G7 nation with a free trade agreement with all the other G7 nations. This is what is building Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the finance minister is absolutely right that Canadians are very educated. They are educated enough to know that the government is cooking the books. The Prime Minister is dividing his deficits on three credit cards. One he calls operational spending, another he claims is investment and a third goes to Crown corporations. However, Canadians understand that just because the Liberals put their debt on three different credit cards does not mean they do not have to pay the interest.
Given that Canadians understand that, when will the Prime Minister get this basic financial lesson?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one thing Canadians understand is that the Leader of the Opposition keeps talking the Canadian economy down. He keeps talking against the industries in this country.

We have the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We have the lowest net debt-to-GDP ratio in the G7. We have one of the lowest deficits in the G7. We are the only country with Germany in the G7 to have an AAA credit rating.
We are going to build Canada strong and we are going to do it with all Canadians.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is the Liberal government that is driving the Canadian economy down. It is doing it with credit card debt, and the interest on it is not free. It comes with interest.

What is the biggest expense in this Liberal budget? Is it health care? Is it seniors? No, the fastest-growing expense is interest on the debt. The average family of four will spend $6,000 on federal taxes just for the debt, not for health care and not for our military.
How does the Prime Minister expect a family to spend $6,000 when they cannot afford groceries?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this is what the Prime Minister is spending money on: 5,000 new jobs in Churchill Falls, 8,000 new jobs for Contrecoeur, 1,000 new jobs for Nouveau Monde Graphite, 18,000 new jobs at Darlington and 30,000 new jobs at Pickering.
Rather than talk down the economy, why do the Conservatives not help us add new jobs to the Canadian economy?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Pierre Poilievre (Leader of the Opposition, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, debt interest is the fastest-growing item on this government's budget. It does not buy a single doctor, a single soldier or a single protection at our border.

Here is what this rising cost means for a family of four. Five years ago, it was $2,400 in interest on the debt for that family. Right now, it is $6,000, and in four years, it will be $8,000 in taxes paid not to get any services but just to pay the bankers.
Will the Prime Minister come to the finance committee and tell that family where they are going to get $8,000 for interest to his banker friends?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. François-Philippe Champagne (Minister of Finance and National Revenue, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, one would expect that after 20 years in this House, the Leader of the Opposition would read The Fiscal Monitor. If he took the time to read it, he would see that public debt charges are at 1.7%, one of the historical lows we have seen in Canada and well below the 6.5% in the 1990s.
Canada has the strongest fiscal position in the G7. We are going to use that to build this country, help Canadians and defend our sovereignty. We are going to build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, Bill C-39 is a major departure. It allows pipeline projects to bypass environmental impact assessments. It would allow swaths of our territory to be designated as being of national interest, thereby suspending the application of environmental laws. It also limits consultations to one year. This means that Ottawa could build the Marinvest pipeline in Quebec without an environmental impact assessment, by suspending environmental laws and rushing through consultations with first nations.
Do the Liberals realize that they are gearing up for a social acceptability crisis?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Dominic LeBlanc (President of the King’s Privy Council for Canada and Minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade, Intergovernmental Affairs, Internal Trade, and One Canadian Economy, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I understand that our colleague from the Bloc Québécois wishes to characterize a series of decisions in a way that is not entirely accurate, but as we have said many times in the House, the bill before Parliament is specifically intended to expedite, in a responsible and rigorous manner, projects that are in the country's economic and social interest.

Just because we are moving faster does not mean we are not meeting our environmental standards or fulfilling our obligations to first nations. On the contrary, we are going to do things the right way.

Mr. Speaker, 15 young people aged 26 or younger are suing the federal government. They accuse the government of jeopardizing their future by failing to take action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. The Prime Minister has answered them by tabling Bill C‑39, which seeks to build pipelines by circumventing environmental standards. His response is to lock them into fossil fuels for at least 50 years. Young people are right to say that the Liberals are jeopardizing their future.
Instead of fighting these young people, why do they not correct course?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Quebec youth, like young people across Canada, dream of a future where the country continues to grow, develop and evolve.

The Churchill Falls project alone is going to create thousands of jobs, and as the largest renewable energy project in North American history, it is going to prove that projects can get done faster without lowering our standards or expectations as Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C‑39 is also an attack on workers' rights.

The Liberals are curtailing the right to strike through their interpretation of section 107 of the Canada Labour Code. The Canadian Union of Public Employees has already announced its intention to challenge this decision in court. The Canadian Labour Congress argues that it undermines decades of job stability. Another trade union has warned that it could encourage employers to bargain in bad faith. Quite simply, the minister has succeeded in uniting everyone—against her.
Does she finally realize that she needs to go back and do her homework?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, with its provisions reforming the Canada Labour Code, Bill C-39 does exactly the opposite. The Minister of Jobs will now have to take certain caveats into account to ensure that section 107 is only applied in specific situations. This is the very opposite of a ban on the right to strike. It is, in fact, a recognition of the constitutional right to strike in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer has warned Canadians that the new finance minister and Prime Minister will not even meet their own fiscal targets and anchors. The Prime Minister, that is, refuses to meet the standards he has imposed on himself and promised. If the Prime Minister is continuing to break these promises, they are about as unreliable as previous prime minister Justin Trudeau's fiscal promises.
Will the Prime Minister confirm that he himself approved using the credit card to run up the deficit?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, that member's leader has been in the House for 8,100 days. He has produced nothing but negativity and divisiveness, and he never has a plan.

When someone is a leader, they can throw their hands up and deny and blame everyone else. A real leader is going to get things done. What about half a trillion dollars through the Canada investment summit? What about non-U.S. exports doubling over the next decade? What about the highest level of foreign investment in our country in decades? On this side of the House, we have a plan. That leader can continue with empty parking lot press conferences and rhetoric.
Mr. Speaker, I happen to think the members of Parliament from multiple parties who have spent decades in this place have made valuable contributions to this country.

The fastest-growing expense in this budget is interest on the debt. In fact, in just a few years, almost 14¢ of every dollar earned by the government will go to paying interest on the debt. When the Prime Minister came in, that number was just over 10¢.

On behalf of all of the young people who will be saddled with the credit card-like spending and debts and deficits of the Liberal government, I ask, why do the Liberals keep breaking their fiscal promises?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Wayne Long (Secretary of State (Canada Revenue Agency and Financial Institutions), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I will say that in 8,100 days, the Leader of the Opposition did build six affordable houses. My riding's hockey team, the Saint John Sea Dogs, has gone to almost as many Memorial Cups as that.

On this side of the House, we have a plan to build our economy. We have a plan to direct investment in major projects and to increase jobs. We have a Prime Minister with world-class economic and business credentials. The Conservative leader has never worked one day outside this House. Canadians see it. Canadians know it. They stand with our side.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister is acting like a gambler hiding his debts from his family. He hides $300 billion of debt in Crown corporations and call it an asset. He calls $19 billion in subsidies and tax credits an investment. He shreds the debt-to-GDP ratio and invents a new one. Every dollar the Liberal government borrows must ultimately be paid back, and it is paid back with dollars earned by and taken from hard-working Canadians.
When will the Prime Minister stop playing accounting games and tell us how he is going to repay his credit card budget?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rechie Valdez (Minister of Women and Gender Equality and Secretary of State (Small Business and Tourism), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, our government is focused on affordability. Just a few weeks ago, 12 million Canadians across the country received the additional deposit of the national groceries and essentials benefit. This is helping curb the cost of everyday essentials and groceries. We have also cut taxes for 22 million Canadians. We are going to continue to be there to support them each and every day.
Mr. Speaker, the Liberals are building a mountain of debt. My generation and my children's generation are going to be crushed under it and the Liberals do not seem to care.

Interest is the fastest-growing expense in the government. It is not health care, infrastructure or defence; it is interest. The Prime Minister is mortgaging our country's future but making the book so confusing that no Canadian can see what the bill actually is. Balancing the budget and repaying Liberal debt would cost each household another $14,000 in taxes each year for a decade.
When will the Prime Minister explain how he is going to repay—
The hon. minister.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Rechie Valdez (Minister of Women and Gender Equality and Secretary of State (Small Business and Tourism), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I said, the national groceries and essentials benefit has helped benefit Canadians right across the country. In fact, in our province of Ontario, the national groceries and essentials benefit has helped five million Ontarians, including in the member's riding.
We are going to cut taxes for them. We are going to support them along the way, while creating good jobs and investing in Canadians as well. We will continue to be there to support them.

Mr. Speaker, what do a leaky roof, a growing credit card bill and Canada have in common? The longer we ignore the problem, the more expensive it gets. Our economy is barely growing, borrowing is way up, and interest rates are on the rise. The Prime Minister promised to put the brakes on spending, but instead he is racking up crazy credit card debt.
If his plan is working, why do 12.5 million Canadians, one in three people, need a grocery assistance benefit just to put food on the table?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Gregor Robertson (Minister of Housing and Infrastructure and Minister responsible for Pacific Economic Development Canada, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, on behalf of our colleagues here, I want to congratulate the new government of B.C., the premier-elect and his team.
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
Order.
The member may continue.
Mr. Speaker, I thank outgoing Premier Eby and his team.

To speak directly to the question from the member opposite, this government is focused on delivering on affordability, whether that is through tax cuts on income tax, the groceries and essentials benefit or the fuel excise tax. We have brought down the costs. We have seen rents come down for 24 months in a row. We are delivering on affordability. There is a lot more work to do. We could use some support from the Conservatives rather than them ranting and raving about it.

Mr. Speaker, the Parliamentary Budget Officer's report is damning for the Liberal government. A deficit of more than $330 billion is projected over five years. Meanwhile, interest on the debt will be over $60 billion next year. That is money that will never be used to help Quebec and Canadian families who are struggling to make ends meet. The Liberals are spending recklessly, but it is Canadians who are paying the price.
When will the government get its spending under control and stop using our children's and grandchildren's credit cards?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am left completely perplexed when I hear the Conservatives talk so much about inflationary programs without ever defining what an inflationary program is. Is it, for example, the 219,416 children in Quebec who receive more than $800 million through the Canada child benefit every year to help their families pay their bills? Is that an inflationary program? The Conservatives voted against that.
Mr. Speaker, what Canadians want is to have money in their pockets from a good job. That is what they need, not cheques from the government.

On Friday, the Minister of Finance was bragging about the economic situation. The Parliamentary Budget Officer just trimmed her outlook for growth to 0.9%, and inflation is projected to be 2.8%. While the minister is patting himself on the back, families are struggling to make ends meet.

I would invite the minister to take a look at the front page of the Journal de Québec. The number of requests for food assistance is skyrocketing. That is what life is like under the Liberals. They need to stop racking up endless debt.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Joël Lightbound (Minister of Government Transformation, Public Works and Procurement and Quebec Lieutenant, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, hearing the member speak like that, I can understand exactly why Quebeckers rejected the Conservative approach. On this side of the House, we believe that we can grow the economy with major projects, such as the high-speed rail project, the Contrecoeur port project, the Nouveau Monde Graphite project and the Port of Québec project. We also believe that the government has a role to play in ensuring that the most vulnerable people get the help they need. Some of the ways we are doing that include a tax cut, the Canada child benefit, the Canadian dental care plan, the Canada groceries and essentials benefit and the national school food program. These are all measures that the Conservatives voted against but that make a real difference for millions of Quebeckers and Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister travelled to Turkey to strike a deal with President Erdoğan's authoritarian regime. He stated that Canada and Turkey have shared values, including “human rights, individual freedoms, democracy, and the rule of law”. The fact of the matter is that the Turkish regime persecutes LGBTQ+ people. It imprisons political opponents and journalists. It is massacring the Kurdish minority. I could keep going.
How can the Prime Minister use the reputation of Quebec and Canada to trivialize that regime's transgressions?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mona Fortier (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we firmly believe that every individual deserves to live with dignity, to feel safe, and to be free to be themselves. Canada will never turn a blind eye to discrimination, persecution or oppression based on sexual orientation or gender identity.
Engagement does not imply approval.
However, by diversifying our partnerships through trade, investment and economic co-operation, we are creating opportunities to strengthen high-level ties and advance human rights.
Mr. Speaker, speaking of hypocrisy, this morning, Canada signed a joint statement condemning the genocide-like violence in Sudan that is being committed by the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF.

Who is the primary supplier of military equipment to the RSF? It is the United Arab Emirates, whose crown prince the Prime Minister of Canada is hosting tonight. This morning, Canada condemned the massacres, but tonight, it is hosting a banquet in honour of one of the people responsible.
Once again, Canada is downplaying human rights abuses.
Will the Prime Minister at least raise this issue at his event tonight?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mona Fortier (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as I said earlier, we firmly believe that everyone deserves to live with dignity, to feel safe and to be free to be themselves. We are continuing our efforts to work with the United Arab Emirates and we will continue those conversations.
In fact, the Prime Minister will be meeting with the U.A.E. team today, and we will see how we can continue to work together.

Mr. Speaker, this is heartbreaking. Right now, in Bradford and in towns and cities across Canada, every shelf in the food bank is bare. Despite the continued generosity of the community, food banks cannot keep up with demand. This is the consequence of Liberal failures that have seen food prices keep soaring, far outpacing what everyday Canadians can afford. People should not have to rely on government or charity just to put a meal on the table.
When will the Prime Minister reverse his inflationary policies so that Canadians can afford to eat again?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, those same Canadians are asking when the Conservatives are going to change their approach. When are they going to start standing up and supporting the government when we put forward initiatives like the groceries and essentials benefit and the Canada child benefit? We stand up and support a national school food program that serves food in the member's communities, but he still stands up and votes against it time and time again, against the very Canadians who benefit from the support the government is working to deliver.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberals can pretend that their expensive programs are working, but the record numbers of Canadians lined up at food banks can tell us that they are not. Food bank usage in Canada has a record 2.35 million visits in a month, and nearly one in five clients is employed. These are working Canadians who used to make ends meet and now cannot because of the government's failed policy.
If the Prime Minister thinks life is so affordable, why is a full-time job not enough to feed a family?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Leslie Church (Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretaries of State for Labour, for Seniors, and for Children and Youth, and to the Minister of Jobs and Families (Persons with Disabilities), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we know that Canadians are facing challenges right now. Food is the beginning, but this also extends to the work we are doing to bring down the cost of renting or buying a home, one of the highest expenses that we know Canadians face. We have renewed our child care deals to keep building a program that is saving families thousands of dollars a year. We are making massive investments in students, in training and in the skilled trades. We are investing in the things that are going to build prosperity and build a bright future for all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal government is costing Canadians more. In 2026, food banks in Alberta have seen more than 230,000 visits. This represents a staggering 9% increase from last year alone. These numbers should alarm every Canadian.
Will the Liberals acknowledge that relying on food banks is now the new normal for Canadians, or are they totally out of touch?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Maninder Sidhu (Minister of International Trade, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, when times are uncertain, our government shows up. It is why residents in the member's riding and those across Canada are receiving the groceries and essentials benefit, receiving close to $1,890 this year.
That is not all. We are leaning in. We are supporting them with child care and supporting them with dental care. We are investing in Canadians, and that is how we build Canada strong.

Mr. Speaker, the face of poverty is changing, and not for the better. People who were donating to food banks a few years ago are now in need of help themselves. Working individuals and dual-income families are being forced to seek food assistance. Six years ago, the Moisson Québec food bank in Quebec City was serving 35,000 people. Now it is serving 84,000 and 35% of them are children.

The Minister of Finance is preparing the budget that he is going to table in a few days. Could he rise and explain to Canadians why they are having such a hard time making ends meet after 11 years of Liberal governance?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anna Gainey (Secretary of State (Children and Youth), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, this year, we made the school food and nutrition program permanent for children across the country. We achieved a participation rate of 80% of public schools across the country, and we are serving meals to 400,000 more children. This investment will continue in the coming years, but every time there is a vote in the House to support this program, the members opposite vote against this investment in children's nutrition.
Mr. Speaker, more than three million Quebeckers need help and food assistance, among other things.

In my region, in my riding, the charitable organization Amélie et Frédérick has seen a 50% increase in demand over the past three years. I received a message from this organization just a few minutes ago, saying that it is getting more and more requests from people aged 75 plus and even 80 plus. These are people who have worked their entire lives and contributed to our society, but who now have to ask for food assistance so they can get enough to eat.
Once again, can the Minister of Finance explain why, after 11 years of Liberal management, seniors are still struggling to get by?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anna Gainey (Secretary of State (Children and Youth), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the Canada child benefit is helping 12,700 families in my colleague's riding. The members opposite vote against that program every single budget. In addition, more than 20,000 people in my colleague's riding are receiving dental care, but he votes against this investment in dental care for children.
We are here for families and for Canadians. We are helping those who need it. It would be nice if the members opposite would stand with us and support us in these measures.
Mr. Speaker, many families in Scarborough—Agincourt and across Canada are concerned about the cost of living and managing expenses such as child care.
Can the Secretary of State for Children and Youth provide an update on what the government is doing to make life more affordable for families?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Anna Gainey (Secretary of State (Children and Youth), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague from Scarborough—Agincourt for her advocacy.
We are working with the provinces and territories across the country to deliver affordable child care that works for families. Fees are down across the country, saving families thousands of dollars.

We know there is more to do, which is why we recently announced a four-year extension with the Province of Ontario, a $12-billion investment in early learning and child care. In the province of Ontario, 39,000 new spots have been created, and we will continue to work with Ontario to deliver on the goal of 86,000 new affordable child care spaces.
Mr. Speaker, 10 months ago, the industry minister promised that she was going to sue Stellantis and get the jobs back. Did she sue? No. Did she get the jobs back? No.
Guess what. The industry minister is now saying that she is going to sue Stelco and get the jobs back. Has she sued? No. Has she got the jobs back? No.
When will the minister stop the talk and get results? Does her word to workers actually mean anything?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, have the Conservatives ever denounced the American tariffs? No. Have they done anything to prevent them from hurting us? No. That is why we need to make sure we have our eyes wide open when dealing with Stellantis and when dealing with Stelco.
When it comes to Stelco, we will do everything to bring the jobs back. There are 11 days left. The clock is ticking, and we will make sure to protect jobs.

Mr. Speaker, did the minister say anywhere in that answer that she was really going to sue? No. It is all talk and no results with the Liberals. She went on a diatribe about a whole bunch of things that the opposition should do in the face of American tariffs. Here is news for the minister: They are the government. They are the one who are supposed to do something about it.
I will go back to this: Does the minister's word actually mean anything? At the expiration of her second 15-day notice, will she sue, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, yes.

Mr. Speaker, it has been a month since Stelco announced that 350 Hamilton steelworkers would lose their jobs. Here is the Conservative five-point plan to protect the steel industry and its workers: get a steel deal with the U.S., which the Prime Minister promised a year and a half ago; end illegal foreign steel dumping; get rid of the industrial carbon tax; pre-approve multiple LNG projects; and sue Cleveland-Cliffs for breaking its contract to the Prime Minister.
Which of these have you completed?
I want to get this straight so that everybody understands. We address questions through the Chair.
The hon. Minister of Industry.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I love it when the Conservatives quote from our plan. It just validates us even more.
Jokes aside—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
I cannot hear. I need to hear this.
The hon. Minister of Industry.

Mr. Speaker, my colleague just referred to how we can support our steelworkers. Our steelworkers are victims of the American tariffs, and we have been there to support them. That is why we will make sure we protect the jobs in Hamilton.

Stelco needs to get back to us in 11 days. The CEO cannot say that he will advocate for American tariffs at a time when he committed to making sure that our steel would go south of the border tariff-free.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister broke his promise of getting a steel deal. The Liberals continue to allow the illegal dumping of foreign steel into the Canadian market. The Liberals refuse to cut the industrial carbon tax so that it is less expensive to work, produce and invest in Canada. The Liberals could take action today by taking Cleveland-Cliffs to court as they said they would. The Liberals' lack of action makes Canada look weak.
Will Canada continue to get bullied by Trump and his buddies, or will the Prime Minister file the lawsuit today?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we have started the legal process under the Investment Canada Act. Under the Investment Canada Act, we need to send a demand letter. The demand letter is supported by true evidence. Of course, we can provide it to the Conservatives if they want. It is 15 pages long with all the evidence.

The undertakings are clear. We need to make sure that Cleveland-Cliffs protects the jobs at the Hamilton and Lake Erie facilities, but it also needs to abide by the commitment of advocating in favour of tariff-free access. It cannot have its cake and eat it too.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister told the European Parliament that people from the EU should be able to live, work and study in Canada. He said this in Europe before telling this Parliament or Canadians anything about it.

The Prime Minister's immigration levels are already outpacing our housing, our health care and our jobs, so I have three questions for him. How many more non-citizens will this new EU deal bring to Canada? Will they count in the levels plan? What will the impact be on our hospitals, housing and social services?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Canadians need to know that we are in control of our own destiny and that we are focused on balance and controlling our immigration system. Canada is working on a deeper transatlantic partnership that will give us more independence in a changing world, and as the Prime Minister said in Strasbourg, nobody will dictate Canada's future. We will always do what is right for Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, nobody believes that immigration is in control in Canada.

Canada already has an existing free trade deal with Europe called CETA. Under CETA, labour mobility is strictly limited to very specific categories of EU citizens for short, defined periods. CETA explicitly does not grant access to the general labour market or allow permanent residence for people in the EU. Now, a leaked document suggests that the Prime Minister is planning to remove CETA's narrow safeguards in this bid for a greater integration with the EU. Given the EU's current open border crisis, this is a very bad idea.
Will the Prime Minister commit to everyone in this place that he will not lift CETA's migration standards?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Maninder Sidhu (Minister of International Trade, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, CETA is something that we should all celebrate. After 10 long years, trade with the European Union is up by over 75%—
Some hon. members: Oh, oh!
The hon. Minister of International Trade, from the beginning.

Mr. Speaker, we just celebrated 10 years of CETA. In fact, two-way trade is up by over 75%. Service is up by over 90%. We have much more room to grow through our digital trade agreement, which we are negotiating right now and will unlock another $5 billion of export opportunities. This is what it means to continue to grow our economy and build Canada strong.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, Europe's open border policies went so badly that they had to adopt a migration pact, which requires countries to take asylum claimants or pay a massive fine, and now the Prime Minister is telling foreign parliaments and foreign newspapers that he is going to have greater immigration levels from the EU. The immigration minister will not give Canadians any details, but Canadians deserve transparency.
How many more non-citizens will this deal bring to Canada, and what will that mean for Canadian hospitals, housing, jobs and social services?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Maninder Sidhu (Minister of International Trade, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the European Union presents a lot of opportunities to Canadian workers and businesses. In fact, we have talked to chambers of commerce and boards of trade across the country that are looking at more opportunities in energy, technology, digital trade and financial services. The European Union presents billions of dollars of opportunities for our export markets, and that is what we will be pursuing.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Michelle Rempel Garner (Calgary Nose Hill, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I think it is very telling that the Prime Minister will not even let his immigration minister give basic details about an open borders pact with the EU. If he has nothing to hide, why will he not let her stand up? The reality is he made an announcement in the European parliament. He is not giving our press gallery details about it in our papers or in interviews here.

Canadians deserve answers. How many more non-citizens will come into the country? What will be the categories of non-citizens and what does this mean for provinces, like Alberta or Quebec, that are asking for more control over immigration levels?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Steven MacKinnon (Minister of Transport and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there is not and will not be an open borders pact with the European Union. What there will be is an enhanced relationship, which will keep this country on track to more than double its non-U.S. trade in the next decade. That will happen. We will have better and closer relations with our European partners. We will have closer economic ties. We will send more Canadian products, farm products and energy products, to Europe, and we will absolutely continue to work with our cousins in the European Union to keep moving forward.
Mr. Speaker, it is high time that the Liberals and the Prime Minister explained the Liberals' gross hypocrisy on immigration.

Over the course of 11 years, the Liberals dismantled a system that was working well. The Prime Minister told the New York Times, but not the House, that it is time to increase immigration. Meanwhile, he is drawing closer to the European Union, which, coincidentally enough, has also lost control of immigration and lost track of millions of people.

What is the agreement with the European Union? Is Canada deporting immigrants who follow the rules because ministers have mishandled the file, all to make room for more immigrants from the European Union?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Lena Metlege Diab (Minister of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what Canadians need to know is that we are masters in our own house. We are focusing on maintaining balance and control over our immigration system.

Just as the Prime Minister said in Strasbourg, no one dictates the path Canada should take. Canada is working to establish a closer transatlantic partnership that will give us greater independence in a changing world.
Mr. Speaker, 90% of Canada's primary aluminum is produced in Quebec. The industry is much more than an economic driver; for our country, it is a strategic industry.
Can the Minister of Industry tell us how our government is projecting jobs and defending Quebec's aluminum industry?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Mélanie Joly (Minister of Industry and Minister responsible for Canada Economic Development for Quebec Regions, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my colleague from Rivière-des-Mille-Îles for her very important question.

Aluminum is one of our industrial strengths. We are proud of our workers in Saguenay—Lac-Saint-Jean and across the country. Last Friday, I was in La Baie to announce a $160-million investment in Rio Tinto and Alouette, two of our major aluminum plants.
We are going to keep helping the large producers, but also the small ones, which are being hit hard by the tariff war. We are going to turn this crisis into an opportunity—
The hon. member for Calgary Signal Hill.

Mr. Speaker, we all want Canada to grow and diversify its export markets. Today, I have good news. Strathcona Resources, a Canadian oil and gas producer, wants to export 250,000 barrels a day of crude oil from Prince Rupert. Strathcona will ship by rail existing in place today. It just needs the Liberal government to get out of the way and remove the west coast tanker ban. My private member's bill, Bill C-264, will do exactly that.
Will the Prime Minister get out of the way and repeal the tanker ban so Strathcona can help Canada become an energy superpower?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, here is what we will do. We will work with B.C., Alberta and affected first nations to build the Pacific link, which will massively increase oil exports. We will also work with first nations to build interties between New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, to build hydro in Quebec, to build nuclear in Ontario and to build the north coast transmission line in B.C.
Rather than fight against indigenous peoples, why do the Conservatives not help us build Canada?

Mr. Speaker, it was Bill C-48 that killed the indigenous-owned Eagle Spirit Energy project, so the member opposite had better reconsider his position on those issues. It is time for the Liberal government to ban the tanker ban and not leave it merely open for consideration. How about repealing it completely so that producers like Strathcona can build our energy industry and bring jobs and prosperity to Canada?
Will the Liberals get out of the way, remove the tanker ban and let Strathcona Resources export a quarter of a million barrels of oil?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, we will up the member by four and get a million barrels a day to the west coast by working in partnership with first nations, not against them. Maybe he could start working with us to build jobs in Canada in partnership with first nations.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister talks about making Canada an energy superpower, yet he continues to stand in the way. Strathcona Resources has a proposal to ship up to 250,000 barrels of Canadian oil a day by rail to Prince Rupert, with exports to overseas markets to begin in as little as two years. The railway already exists. The company is ready to pursue the project. What is missing is to repeal the Liberal tanker ban.
Will the Liberals finally get out of the way, remove the tanker ban and allow Strathcona Resources to move forward with this proposal, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Tim Hodgson (Minister of Energy and Natural Resources, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, it is very interesting that the member is focused on something in B.C. Maybe she should focus a little closer to home. Her premier, Premier Wakeham, said that the federal government was instrumental in getting Bay du Nord built, a $10-billion energy project in her province that the Conservatives are not helping support. Maybe they should figure out where they should spend their time.
Mr. Speaker, food insecurity is not just a problem for Canadians. It is a global challenge. No matter one's circumstances, everyone deserves access to safe, nutritious food.

In my riding of Spadina—Harbourfront, local food banks, such as Spadina-Fort York Community Care at the Waterfront Neighbourhood Centre, work tirelessly to support our community. The local food infrastructure fund has been an integral tool for supporting these organizations and earlier this year, our government announced a new $20-million community support stream.
Can the minister please update the House on how this funding will be distributed across the country and the impact it is going to have for Canadians?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Heath MacDonald (Minister of Agriculture and Agri-Food, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, the government is taking immediate action through the groceries and essentials benefit, through the school of food program and through the local food infrastructure fund community support stream. Food Banks Canada and Second Harvest will both receive up to $10 million. These two recipients will distribute that food to eligible food banks and not-for-profit, community-based organizations across the country.
We are focused on the present, but we are also building our national food security strategy for the future.

Mr. Speaker, families in Richmond Centre—Marpole are concerned. With just days before the October 29 deadline to appeal the B.C. Supreme Court's ruling on drug trafficking, the Liberal government still owes Canadians an answer. What are they waiting for, the Public Prosecution Service? The tail should not wag the dog. The Attorney General has the authority to direct an appeal.
Will the Liberals exercise their authority to protect Canadian families from drug traffickers, or is there something the Liberals do not want Canadians to know?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Ruby Sahota (Secretary of State (Combatting Crime), Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, traffickers cause real harm. That is why we have been working hard to make sure they get serious punishments. We have passed many different Criminal Code reforms in this House.
As for the appeal, we will let the Public Prosecution Service make its decision. It still has time, and I trust that it will make a good decision.

Mr. Speaker, today first nations chiefs are in Ottawa at the first nations-first ministers meeting. A main topic of concern is Bill C-39, which first nations across the country have called to be withdrawn, including BCAFN, UBCIC,Treaty 6, Onion Lake, NAN, COO, APNQL and the Iroquois Confederacy representing hundreds of thousands of first nations. Chiefs have been clear that the success of this meeting will be judged by the Liberal government's actions.
The resource minister says that he respects indigenous rights, so will he withdraw Bill C-39 now, yes or no?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Jaime Battiste (Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Crown-Indigenous Relations, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I have good news for the member. Right now, first nations are meeting with premiers from across this country and our government in one of the most historic first ministers meetings with first nations. First nations shaped the agenda for this meeting and we value the opportunity to hear directly from the leaders addressing their concerns and having honest conversations about the opportunities and challenges ahead.
We are doing historic and important things in Canada and indigenous people will be important in shaping this future together.
I wish to draw the attention of members to the presence in the gallery of the Hon. Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, Minister of Foreign Affairs for the Republic of Ghana.
Some hon. members: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present, in both official languages, the 36th report of the Standing Committee on Procedure and House Affairs. The committee advises that, pursuant to Standing Order 91.1(2), the Subcommittee on Private Members' Business met to consider the orders for the second reading of private members' bills originating in the Senate, and recommended that the items listed herein, which it has deemed should not be designated non-votable, be considered by the House.
Pursuant to Standing Order 91.1(2), the report is deemed adopted.
Mr. Speaker, today I rise to present two petitions.

The first petition calls on the government to suspend staff terminations at Agriculture and Agri-Foods Canada and to continue operating the research centre, research farms and the organic and regenerative research program for at least 24 months to provide cost-benefit transparency and to ensure that irreplaceable research capacity and long-term studies are not lost due to hasty decisions.
The petitioners are urging not to base our good public health decisions on political sound bites. They have to be based on research.

The second petition comes from my constituents in Winnipeg Centre who are expressing their concern with the government's ongoing violation of international law by its refusal to close the loopholes in Canada for weapons exports that enable Canadian-made arms to be used for war crimes and genocide. My constituents call on the government to fulfill the end of peace and to close this loophole once and for all.
I will always support my constituents in upholding international law, and I join them in demanding that the Liberal government do the same.
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to table a petition on behalf of wildland firefighters. It is timely, as representatives from the BC General Employees' Union and NUPGE are here in town.

The petitioners cite that, across Canada, wildland firefighters perform life-threatening public safety duties, including wildfire suppression, evacuations and the protection of communities, ecosystems, property and critical infrastructure during increasingly severe wildfire seasons.

Petitioners highlight that, despite performing the same dangerous work as other firefighters, wildland firefighters are excluded from the firefighter category in the national occupational classification, which is a misclassification that limits their access to recognition, benefits and protections available to other firefighters and public safety workers. This recognition has been afforded to wildland firefighters working directly with the federal government as well as to other firefighters across the country, allowing them to fight for the appropriate workforce protections and benefits they need as firefighters, first responders and public safety personnel.

Petitioners also highlight that the House of Commons Standing Committee on Public Safety and National Security unanimously supported the action to address this inequity but that no corrective action has been taken so far.

The petitioners want the government to immediately correct the misclassification of wildland firefighters in the national occupational classification by recognizing them as firefighters, and remove any and all federal barriers that prevent wildland firefighters from being recognized as the firefighters and public safety workers that they are.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I ask that all questions be allowed to stand at this time.
Is that agreed?

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-40, An Act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, a riot broke out on Friday, October 16, 2026, at La Macaza Institution, in my riding, caused by understaffing. Frontline officers found themselves in the middle of what could have been a very dangerous situation. I want all my colleagues who were not aware of this situation to know that it was very alarming. Without the expertise of the officers on the ground, the situation could have ended very differently.

The connection I want to make here is obvious. Let me be very clear. The inmate population at La Macaza has changed in recent years. We are not talking about a junior kindergarten here. We are not talking about a day care centre. We are talking about a prison, the La Macaza institution.

This is a direct result of the federal government's policies. As everyone knows, the government chose to cut $132 million from Correctional Service Canada. These $132 million in cuts come on top of budget cuts being made across the public service.

Now we are learning that under Bill C-40, the Crown corporation the government wants to establish would have a friend of the Prime Minister, Doug Guzman, as its CEO. Is anyone surprised? Mr. Guzman, a former Goldman Sachs executive and banker like the Prime Minister, is expected to get a salary in the neighbourhood of $700,000 a year. That is a little higher than what an MP or even a minister earns. I am outraged.

While staff on the ground work day in, day out to ensure public safety at the prisons in La Macaza, Joliette, Cowansville and Port-Cartier, they are seeing how budget cuts have a direct impact on their work. We are being asked, as parliamentarians, to vote to give a $700,000 salary to a friend of the Prime Minister. This is no joke. That is the reality and it is insulting.

I will explain why. It is because we also learned that Mr. Guzman allegedly threatened to leave the Defence Investment Agency, and that it was as a result of this blackmail that the government decided to make the agency into a Crown corporation. Agency officials testified to this at the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates.

I want to explain to Quebeckers and Canadians what this change really means. The creation of a Crown corporation means establishing a company that is independent from government with a board of directors and a chief executive officer. The Crown corporation will not be accountable to Parliament. I want to emphasize that: It will not be accountable to Parliament. The government will not be responsible for its day-to-day operations.

As everyone knows, Canada already has plenty of Crown corporations, including the CBC, the Business Development Bank of Canada, Destination Canada and Canada Post. What do those Crown corporations have in common? They provide services. They have mandates aimed at serving the public or businesses. However, the management of military and defence procurement is not a social, cultural or economic development mandate. There is no rational argument to justify the creation of a Crown corporation in this case.

The only reason I can see is that the government wants to do as it did with Bill C-5 this spring or, worse, Bill C-39. The government and the Prime Minister want free rein to ram this through and control the whole process without any parliamentary oversight. Now that is power.

What the Prime Minister wants is to evade legislative oversight and turn Parliament into a rubber stamp. It is easy. No one says a word, and his plans go off without a hitch. His actions go unnoticed. There is no accountability, period.

Members of Parliament are being denied three roles. I have been here for seven years and I must say I have never seen anything like this. The first is the role of intermediary between citizens and the public administration. The second is the role of legislator. The third is the role of overseeing and monitoring government actions.

Otherwise, what is the point? How will lawmakers—and I am talking about all of us, not just the opposition—be able to hold the government accountable if the government keeps undermining transparency and accountability? It is troubling.

With Bill C-40, just as with Bill C-39, we are witnessing undemocratic manoeuvres to ram through measures without parliamentary scrutiny. They want to rush this through, quietly and without anyone noticing, as I have already mentioned. What would be my role on the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates if I no longer had the right to scrutinize these matters, if I no longer had the right to know? What do we have to offer to all the people who elected us?

I represent the riding of Laurentides—Labelle. I represent a geographical area, but above all I represent people. My riding is home to 92,897 people. When I rise in the House, I am speaking on their behalf. I am speaking in the interests of my constituents. I am speaking with them in mind.
When the Prime Minister and the government seek to limit parliamentary power, what they are really doing is limiting the power of the people. I think that is clear.

This authoritarian streak worries me, and I am not the only one. I do not want the government to hide behind a board of directors it has appointed in order to justify potentially dubious purchases, or to pat itself on the back when a purchase proves beneficial. I do not want the Government of Canada—which, incidentally, is the only one amongst our allies to have established a system of this sort—to be able to evade the close scrutiny of members of Parliament. We deserve a government that treats Parliament with respect. That is what people want. I want Parliament to be able to work diligently, with respect for the public and with the sound management of public finances in mind.

I am concerned. Efficiency must not come at all costs, yet that is what we are being told. We are being told that the government wants to do this in order to be efficient. We have just seen that we could have been efficient by taking care of our culture and investing in it. However, a one-sided decision was made.
In closing, I agree that the process can certainly be improved. However, we must ensure that the intentions are noble and in the common interest, not in the interest of the Prime Minister's friends.
I have seen this movie before, and I hope that things will be different this time because the situation is serious. Let us treat it seriously.

Mr. Speaker, I read Bill C‑40 and had the opportunity to give a speech here in the House. I think there is a bit of a misunderstanding about the bill. I will explain why. By creating this corporation, Bill C‑40 will provide support so businesses can bid on government contracts. I have worked with businesses. All too often, we see that they would like to bid on contracts, but they lack the financial means or do not have the necessary financial backing, from banks, for instance. That is what Bill C‑40 offers. It will support the entire sector in bidding on these contracts. It will provide loan insurance. It will make it possible to get loans.
I would like my colleague to take the time to read the bill carefully and consider the impact it could have on the sector. It will support hundreds of businesses so they can bid on contracts.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question, because it gives me the opportunity to mention something I did not address in my speech: the role of the procurement ombudsman. The ombudsman serves as an independent safeguard and external watchdog. When a contract is disputed and a clear answer is required, a complaint can be filed with the ombudsman. The ombudsman then appears before the Standing Committee on Government Operations and Estimates, helping us get to the bottom of the matter. We correct course, if necessary. With the Defence Investment Agency, however, there will be no ombudsman. Just imagine: no transparency.

I fully agree with my colleague that we need to speed up the process, that we need to support this sector and give it a helping hand, but at what cost? It must certainly not be at the cost of undermining our democracy.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciated my colleague's comments regarding respect and parliamentary oversight. To what extent is she confident that the Liberal MPs on the committee will accept amendments aimed at guaranteeing parliamentary oversight?

Mr. Speaker, my colleague's French is always outstanding. What we are hearing right now is a lot of lofty rhetoric. As with other files, I would like to know just how aware government members are of what is taking place. I have already spoken about wilful blindness, but ultimately we will be left dealing with the consequences of a major departure, and that worries me. If the government is going to retain all these safeguards and criteria, then what emerges will no longer really be a Crown corporation. The rationale simply does not hold water.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague for her excellent speech. When we look at Bill C‑39, which follows on the heels of Bill C‑5, we see the government concentrating even more power in the Prime Minister's Office by allowing the Prime Minister to designate projects as being in the national interest and circumvent environmental laws. Is Bill C‑40 not simply a continuation of that same trend? How far is this going to go? What does my colleague think about that?

Mr. Speaker, for those who follow our work, this is just the tip of the iceberg. It is unbelievable what is happening. We supposedly have a saviour for now, but what happens later? What then? All of this in the name of national sovereignty and economic development. Seriously, we are undermining our democracy. Bill C-40 is exactly the same anti-transparency process.
Mr. Speaker, in my riding, the beautiful Bay of Quinte, we are proudly home to the Royal Canadian Air Force's primary and largest air mobility hub, 8 Wing at CFB Trenton.

While CFB Trenton is a fascinating and awesome place to celebrate in its sheer enormity and scope of operations, we are here today to discuss important legislation to accelerate defence procurement, strengthen Canadian industry and reinforce Canadian sovereignty. We do so to benefit and bolster the work of the 5,000 military and civilian personnel who keep CFB Trenton operational 24-7, 365 days a year.

Bill C-40, the strengthening Canada's defence sector act, represents a major step in modernizing how Canada equips its military. Above all, the legislation is about building a stronger, more capable Canada, a Canada that can continue to defend itself against emerging threats, protect its interests and keep Canadians safe.

The bill comes at a defining moment in our country's history. Our government is making a generational investment to rebuild, rearm and reinvest in the Canadian Armed Forces, but our investments are only part of the equation. We must also ensure that they translate into effective military capabilities delivered to our Canadian Armed Forces quickly and efficiently, as well as that they deliver real economic benefits for Canadians from coast to coast to coast. To meet these important commitments, in October 2025, we established the Defence Investment Agency, or the DIA, as a special operating agency within Public Services and Procurement Canada.

In just one year, the DIA has helped accelerate and advance a number of major defence projects. The legislation we are proposing builds on this momentum, giving the DIA the additional tools and authorities it needs to keep doing this work even more quickly and efficiently.

It is important to know that we are not starting from zero. With that in mind, I would like to take a few minutes to highlight some of the important projects the DIA has been able to advance over the past year, as well as to discuss how Bill C-40 would ensure that we can keep delivering at the pace that our military needs and that Canadians expect.

Let me begin with air and space. Canada is a vast country. Protecting our airspace, particularly in the Arctic, requires modern aircraft, advanced surveillance systems and reliable communications. We are making significant progress on all three fronts. In May, Canada selected Saab as the preferred supplier for our future airborne early warning and control capability. Negotiations are now advancing toward the acquisition of the GlobalEye system. This system would provide long-range surveillance and early warning capabilities, helping our forces detect and track potential threats. Because GlobalEye uses Canadian-made Bombardier Global 6500 aircraft, this project also offers important opportunities for Canada's aerospace industry.

As we strengthen Canada's air and space capabilities, we are also investing in emerging technologies. In just months, the defence drone initiative, made possible because of DIA involvement, has helped lay the foundations for a sovereign national defence drone ecosystem.

Another important initiative is the enhanced satellite communications project, polar. This project will provide our military with reliable, secure communications in the Arctic, where conventional communications can often be limited.

Working with Canadian industry leaders such as Telesat and MDA, the Defence Investment Agency has helped advance an innovative procurement approach. Rather than developing a technical solution in isolation, we engaged Canadian industry earlier, drawing on its expertise to help identify the best way forward. In August, the agency awarded Telesat a $2.3-billion contract for the first major component of this capability. This is an excellent example of how we can move faster while strengthening Canadian technological expertise and industrial capacity.

Let me turn then to land capabilities. Our soldiers need modern equipment they can depend on. Earlier this year, our government awarded Colt Canada a contract for up to 65,402 new Canadian modular assault rifle systems. These rifles will replace equipment that has served our military for decades. Through the contract negotiated by the DIA, Colt Canada is committed to incorporating at least 80% Canadian content into these rifles, on top of their being built domestically.
This project is a great example of how the DIA is already improving readiness for our soldiers while supporting Canadian manufacturing, skilled workers and our domestic defence industrial base.

Likewise, the DIA is helping Canada move forward on the capabilities the Royal Canadian Navy needs to defend our vast waters, done most notably through the Canadian patrol submarine project. In July, Canada selected Germany-based TKMS, with the support of Germany and Norway, as its preferred supplier. Negotiations are under way to acquire up to 12 modern, conventionally powered submarines with long range, long endurance and Arctic capabilities. These submarines would strengthen our ability to detect, track and deter potential adversaries in the Atlantic, Pacific and Arctic oceans. We are planning to sustain these submarines right here in Canada.

These are just a few examples of the major defence acquisitions under way. We have been able to make significant progress on these projects since the creation of the DIA. They also highlight something important. The DIA's goal is not simply to acquire equipment faster. It is about fundamentally transforming how we approach defence procurement.

Historically, major acquisitions have involved several federal departments, each with important responsibilities: National Defence identified military requirements; Public Services and Procurement Canada managed procurement and contracting; and Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada oversaw industrial and economic considerations. While this arrangement brought valuable expertise across government, it could also create duplication, delays and uncertainty as projects move between organizations.

The DIA is helping to change that. By bringing together military, technical, commercial and procurement specialists from across government, the agency is building integrated teams that can work collaboratively from the earliest stages of a project. The DIA is also introducing more flexible approaches to procurement. That includes engaging industry earlier, streamlining decision-making and considering existing commercial or military solutions where appropriate.

This work is closely connected to Canada's defence industrial strategy, which is helping ensure our defence investments also build the industrial capacity, skilled workforce and secure supply chains needed to produce and sustain critical capabilities here at home. At its heart is a straightforward approach: build, partner, buy. That means to build in Canada where we have the capacity or where developing that capacity is strategically important; partner with trusted allies when collaboration provides access to better capabilities, technologies or production opportunities; and buy existing capabilities from trusted partners.

It would all strengthen our capability to maintain and sustain essential military equipment in Canada. That is important because every critical component we can produce domestically, every system we can maintain and repair ourselves, makes our country more resilient. The DIA would have a clear responsibility for translating these requirements into results, all while maintaining strong governance, financial oversight and accountability to Parliament through a minister.

Ultimately, our success will not be measured by the number of contracts we sign. It will be measured by the opportunities we create for Canadian workers and businesses, and it will be measured by the capabilities we deliver to our military. That is what Bill C-40 is designed to achieve: a stronger military; a stronger defence industry; and a stronger, more sovereign Canada. That is why I urge all members of the House to support the legislation.

Mr. Speaker, the member for Bay of Quinte represents the largest Air Force base in Canada. It is a base that houses our C-17s, a massive equipment procurement that was purchased by the previous Conservative government without this agency, without anything. It was done through a sole-source process. It was done as an operational requirement, and it did not eliminate the need for parliamentary oversight or accountability.

Would the member agree that the purchase, along with the Chinooks and tanks during the war in Afghanistan, were all good purchases that were done for the right reasons, and they were done efficiently and well?
Mr. Speaker, I thank my friend, the member for Bruce—Grey—Owen Sound, for his service to Canada as a veteran, especially at this time of year.

I listened earlier as the member recited a litany of shortages in sending troops into harm's way when he was an active serving member, and I would like to remind him that the program we are introducing in this bill would help address the very concerns he expressed earlier. This program is designed to help better procure items such as C-17, but we have also seen that we need everything from socks to submarines, and this legislation would help do that, not only with speed but also with great oversight.

Mr. Speaker, in my speech earlier, I talked about accountability and transparency. I would like my colleague to explain to me how the government will be able to ensure transparency in this new Crown corporation. I would like him to explain that to me.

Mr. Speaker, in the new legislation, the shift is about centralizing execution and accountability with what is known as the CCDI. While recognizing that major defence investments will continue to advance broader Government of Canada priorities, the CCDI mandate would be more focused on defence production, procurement and investment. It would also accelerate delivery of defence capabilities.

That does not mean there would be less oversight. The CCDI would operate at arm's length under the national defence portfolio, reporting to a new minister, called the associate minister of national defence for procurement. The Government of Canada is committed to clear accountability and a more integrated approach to—
Questions and comments. The hon. member for Compton—Stanstead.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the Bay of Quinte for his speech on the new Defence Investment Agency. I would like my colleague to elaborate on the type of spinoffs there might be for a riding like his or mine.

Mr. Speaker, the DIA would be continue to operate under its existing authorities and advance procurements while the new Crown corporation is established. The transition would be managed to maintain continuity and minimize disruption to ongoing procurements, industrial industry partners and client organizations. Earlier today, I met with a defence contractor, for instance, who is interested and already actively working at CFB Trenton in my riding of the Bay of Quinte. They are very keen on Bill C-40 to see that this exact piece of legislation would help them further bring their private expertise to work in collaboration with our defences.

Mr. Speaker, I noted that, in the member's speech, he said that there would still be accountability through a minister, but with the nature of creating this as a Crown corporation, does he not agree that this would inherently set the operations of this Crown corporation at arm's length from direct ministerial accountability?

Mr. Speaker, as we have seen, we are not reinventing the wheel here. We are not reinventing Crown corporations. I fail to see why, when we are talking defence procurement, we would all of a sudden have less accountability. We have many Crown corporations that operate very closely with government, but that is done with very good scrutiny.

Mr. Speaker, our soldiers need equipment quickly, yet the government has spent the last year trying to decide how to organize the bureaucracy responsible for buying it. After 11 years of Liberal government, our sailors, soldiers and aviators are still being asked to make do with aging equipment while they wait for replacements, and they continue to do their jobs. They deserve a government that will do its job too.

Last October, the Liberals created the Defence Investment Agency. Canadians were told it would cut red tape and get equipment to our Forces faster. A few months later, the government decided the agency needed to become a stand-alone entity. It brought forward legislation in the spring. Now before that legislation is even completed, Bill C-40 proposes turning it into a Crown corporation.

For Canadians unfamiliar with that, a Crown corporation is a government-owned company that has its own board executives, such as Canada Post and Via Rail. That is a lot of time spent reorganizing an agency that was supposed to save time. Why did an agency inside a department not work? Why is the proposal for a stand-alone agency already being replaced? What exactly would a Crown corporation fix that the Liberals could not get right the first two times? The government should answer those questions before asking Parliament to approve another restructuring.

Conservatives have called for one clear point of accountability, with a dedicated secretariat in the Privy Council Office so that military purchases receive priority at the cabinet table. We want decisions made, contracts moving and, most of all, equipment delivered. Canadians should be able to identify who is responsible and hold that person accountable for the results.

The Liberals keep changing their minds about who should buy the equipment, while troops are still expected to do their jobs without it. They cannot put their duties on hold while the government figures out how to do its job. After 11 years, they deserve a government that can get them what they need and do so without delay.

The government keeps restructuring its defence agency rather than delivering equipment to our soldiers.
