The bill should provide for a complete accounting of the available funding mechanisms, the limits on borrowing and guarantees, and the source of funding for equity acquisitions. Parliament should receive regular reports showing how much money has been invested, who has received it, the value of outstanding guarantees, the losses incurred and the returns earned. Canadians should be able to understand what has happened to their money.

Bill C-31 provided for a legislative review within three years. Bill C-40 would extend that period to five years. With that, the government would be creating a more complicated financial institution, while waiting longer to see whether it is working. That should be corrected.

Canada needs a more effective defence procurement system. We need our military to be properly equipped, and we should be developing Canadian industrial capacity wherever it makes strategic and economic sense, but the priority must remain the defence of Canada and the interests of Canadian taxpayers. Governance matters. Many of the provisions I have spoken about today may be quite dry, but they are very important. It is not just conflicts of interest that matter. It is also the appearance of those conflicts.

When government acts as investor, lender, guarantor and customer, the opportunities for private profit can be substantial, and so can the opportunities for financial losses, poor procurement decisions and preferential treatment. The government has decided it wants to use these powers. The responsibility of Parliament now is to ensure that they are exercised under rules that protect the public interest. The Defence Investment Agency should not become a place where private investors get the financial rewards of government decisions while ordinary Canadians are left paying the bills.
I submit that we have opportunities to improve the governance provisions in these bills and that we ought to do exactly that.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I agree wholeheartedly with the member when she says that governance matters. I am an advocate for a Crown corporation because in my years both in opposition and government, I have seen the benefits of a well-run Crown corporation, both at the provincial level and at the federal level. It can provide a high sense of transparency and accountability. When we take a look at the potential mandate for this particular one for military procurement, we see that it is it good not only for Canada's defence but also for our industry as a whole, if done properly.
I would agree with the member's comments that governance is important. Are there changes the member would like to see that could enhance a Crown corporation?

Mr. Speaker, I would submit that if the hon. member had listened to my speech, he would know that I have just proposed a number of very specific measures that I believe would enhance the governance of this particular Crown corporation.
I do agree with him that there are some Crown corporations that have excellent governance mechanisms. At the moment, on the surface of the bill before us, I think there is much room for improvement.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague for her speech, which was, I must say, forceful and very firm.
We know that transforming the Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation means that certain watchdogs, such as the procurement ombud, will not be able to scrutinize its activities.
Is that a concern of my colleague's?
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the member for his question, and I am continuing to work on being able to answer questions in French.

I do agree that there are some significant transparency issues. I am encouraged in some ways by the fact that this is really the third iteration of the organization. However, there have been many concerns around transparency and accountability raised in the chamber thus far, and I would urge the government to pay close attention to them. I think there is substantial and significant work to be done on the bill.

Mr. Speaker, it was not very long ago that BC Ferries awarded a contract to China. That was not in the interests of the Canadian people, and most people we talked to on the street thought it was absolutely ridiculous. Meanwhile, the federal government gave billions of dollars to BC Ferries, but the Liberals just shrugged their shoulders with no regard.

Would allowing this Crown corporation open the door for the Crown corporation to be sucked into the American military complex? We would then have a situation such as BC Ferries, where it would be awarding contracts that the Canadian people may not appreciate.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for the concern he shows for people in my community, who, like the people in his community, are dependent upon ferry services for most of their daily existence. This is one of the reasons I wanted to highlight the importance of the fact that there are currently no invest Canadian provisions in the bill.

Many members have raised issues, and I think a number of them are legitimate. I hope the government is paying attention to these debates and remarks, and that the Liberals will go back to the drawing board and make some improvements to the bill that would enhance the impact of these very important decisions on Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. colleague reads bills carefully. I am wondering if she noted that it is not the Minister of Defence or even the associate minister for defence procurement who is actually named in the bill, but the Liberals will fill in the blanks later from cabinet.
Mr. Speaker, again, it goes to the fact that the bill feels like one that is half-baked.

There are so many possibilities. I go back again to the fact that it would not just be an actual legal conflict of interest that we need to be concerned with. We need to also be concerned about appearances. Right now, I think that the government is actually leaving itself vulnerable to all kinds of unintended consequences if Parliament is not given a chance to have a substantially amended and improved bill.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, there have been discussions among the parties, and if you seek it, I think you will find unanimous consent for the following motion:

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: The House resumed consideration of the motion that Bill C-40, An Act respecting production, procurement and investment in relation to national defence and national security, be read the second time and referred to a committee.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, as always, it is a true honour for me to rise in the House on behalf of the residents of my constituency of Davenport. I am rising to speak to Bill C-40, the strengthening Canada's defence sector act. I am also speaking as the chair of the Canadian NATO Parliamentary Association, and I am very proud also to serve as the vice-president of the NATO parliamentary assembly.

I spend a lot of time with parliamentarians from across our alliance, and what I hear from them helps explain why this bill is so important right now. Let me start with what the bill would actually do.

Bill C-40 has two parts. The first part would establish as a Crown corporation the Defence Investment Agency, which we launched just over a year ago. Its job would be to carry out the production, procurement and investment of defence assets for the Canadian Armed Forces, the Department of National Defence and our NATO allies. Its chief executive officer would report to the board of directors, and the corporation would remain accountable to Parliament through a responsible minister.

The second part of the bill would amend the National Defence Act to create an associate minister of national defence for procurement so that, for the first time, defence procurement would sit under one responsible minister. It would also update the Defence Production Act, which would allow Canada to stockpile critical supplies and to invest directly in our defence and security sectors. This is what is in the bill. I would like to spend the rest of my time talking about why we absolutely need it.

For over 70 years, Canadians have lived within an international order that we helped build after World War II, one based on rules, on open trade and on strong institutions such as NATO and the United Nations. It was never perfect, but it brought us decades of peace and prosperity. That world has changed in a very significant way, and I agree with our Prime Minister when he says, “We are in the midst of a rupture, not a transition.” We are watching the rise of authoritarianism and, in some places, fascism. Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine, and the tariffs imposed by our closest neighbour have hurt Canadian workers and shaken the global economic system that so many of our jobs depend on.

I know that many of the residents in my riding of Davenport are feeling this. When I talk to people at community events or at the door, I hear a real unease, a sense that something fundamental has shifted. To me, they are right to feel this way. I do not think we can afford to be nostalgic for the world as it was. We have to deal with the world as it is today.

One of the biggest changes is in the nature of war itself. Admiral Pierre Vandier, who leads NATO's Allied Command Transformation and recently visited Canada, has been warning that the lines among peace, crisis and war have broken down and that our adversaries are working around the clock, below the threshold of open conflict in what he calls the grey zone. NATO now has a name for this: cognitive warfare. It means our adversaries are not only trying to take territory but are also trying to change how we think, they are trying to divide us and they are trying to make us lose faith in each other and in our democracy.

Let me put it simply: An attack on Canada today may never involve a single soldier crossing our border. It could mean someone stealing our data or our money, spreading disinformation in our communities or trying to get into the systems that run our water and electricity.

Admiral Vandier also said, “The most expensive commodity today is time”, and that line has stayed with me because time is precisely what our current procurement system has been costing us. Canada, as we know, is the second-largest country in the world by land mass, with the longest coastline on earth and an Arctic that is opening up and attracting more and more attention from others. Defending a country this size takes the right equipment, delivered on time. In the past, too often we have not delivered.

Our public servants have worked incredibly hard on these files. The problem, though, is a system that was never built for the speed this world now demands. As a result, our women and men in uniform have too often waited years, sometimes decades, for the equipment they need to do their job. That is why we are proposing a Crown corporation.

The change we need is urgent, and I believe we need a dedicated institution with the authority to deliver it. As a Crown corporation, the agency would be able to negotiate contracts using commercial practices that industry already understands, and it would bring procurement and strategic investment together under a single mandate so decisions can move much faster.
Allies like the United Kingdom, Australia and Sweden have had dedicated defence procurement bodies for years, and this bill would bring Canada in line with all of them.

I know some members of this House will say that a new Crown corporation simply adds more bureaucracy. I would say it does the reverse, because it brings work that is now split across three departments into one place and removes many duplicate approvals. I also want to be clear that accountability matters. The corporation would still follow Treasury Board rules. It would still be audited, it would still report to this House and it would still answer to a minister.

Now, I want to take a moment to speak to a question I often hear from residents of my constituency of Davenport, a community that has always cared deeply about peace and social justice. People often ask me, “Why are we spending so much on defence?”, and whether that money and effort should be going towards peace instead. I want them to know that I share their commitment to peace. Where I have landed is that in today's world, peace has to be protected, and that requires us to be able to defend ourselves. Strong deterrence is often what stops a dangerous situation from turning into a war. I believe that a Canada that can defend its own sovereignty will be a much stronger voice for peace, human rights and diplomacy around the world.

This is also about our responsibility to our allies. Every time I meet with my NATO colleagues, I hear about how much they are counting on Canada to do its part, because collective security only works when every member contributes. I am proud that, for the first time since the end of the Cold War, Canada has met NATO's 2% target, and that we have committed to reaching 5% by 2035. Bill C-40 is how we will make sure that this investment turns into real capability for our forces and our allies, delivered on time.

I also want to mention jobs. Our defence industrial strategy aims to have 70% of defence acquisitions go to Canadian firms and to create up to 125,000 good-paying jobs. Our goal is that when Canada buys, we build here in Canada, using Canadian steel and aluminum, and the talent of Canadian workers. We are already seeing this happen with more than $11 billion for new icebreakers at Chantier Davie in Quebec and with an expanded armoured vehicle fleet that will sustain thousands of jobs in London, Ontario.

Does this mean that all is done? Absolutely not. We have so much more to do, but this bill is one important step, and it gives us the institution we need to get this work done at the speed this moment requires.

My grandparents came to this country in the 1950s, and Canada gave them a safe, free and democratic place to build their lives. I think about that often and about our responsibility to protect what earlier generations built for us, especially now when the world feels so much less certain. I have a lot of confidence in Canadians. I believe we can protect our sovereignty, stand with our allies, grow our economy and continue to be the voice for peace in the world. I believe that Bill C-40 will help us do that.
I urge all members of this House to support this bill, and to send it to committee where we can study it carefully and make it even stronger.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the member for Davenport for laying out a lot of the reasons why we need quality defence equipment for our Canadian Armed Forces and laying out the threat that we face with global instability.

However, the other point I wanted to make was, historically, in the previous Conservative government, there were massive amounts of equipment delivered without the need for a defence investment agency in a very timely fashion, and I felt the benefits of that wholeheartedly.
I want to correct the member a little. She said this bill has two parts, when it actually has three parts. The third part is that this act needs to be reviewed within five years.

Would the member commit to holding the government to account to ensure that review happens, because we have more than 13 pieces of legislation right now that have not been reviewed and that review is overdue?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his extraordinary contribution to our country. I know that he served in the Canadian Armed Forces. He is also heavily involved in the Canadian NATO Parliamentary Association. I always value his voice, his questions and his wisdom as part of our team.

I know the hon. member made a reference how, in the past, this Crown corporation would not have been needed. That is why I spent quite a bit of time in my speech talking about how the world has so transitioned and transformed. We are in the middle of a rupture. We have to do extraordinary things at this particular moment. What I would say to the member is, indeed, we do need this Crown corporation now, and I think I have explained the value of it.
In terms of his question around the third part, and whether we would be open to review, I would say that is why we have committees. It is important for us to discuss these ideas at committee.
Mr. Speaker, I have a very specific question for my colleague.

She praised the new structure a lot, although we think it will be unnecessary. Apart from that, does she not feel a little uncomfortable at the thought that the head of this new structure is going to be paid twice as much as the Minister of Finance and that—to be blunt—this executive used to work with the Prime Minister and is a good friend of his? How does she feel about that?

Mr. Speaker, I want to remind the hon. member about the importance of moving this bill forward to committee. I think there is always room for us to make recommendations if there are areas that we think we need to improve.

I will remind everyone that this bill would help us streamline Canadian defence procurement under a Crown corporation. We would build a system that is faster, more efficient and ready to meet Canada's needs today and into the future.

I would say that in terms of accountability, under the system that we are proposing as part of part 1, the chief executive officer would be accountable to the board of directors for the management and administration of the corporations. It would also be accountable to the Government of Canada through a responsible minister and would have strict financial and reporting requirements, participate in audits and be subject to parliamentary oversight.
Mr. Speaker, Longueuil—Saint‑Hubert has a military base with real soldiers who work extremely hard to protect our territorial sovereignty with known expertise in the defence sector.
How will this legislation enable our businesses to contribute more to keeping Canada safe while stimulating the local economy and creating good jobs for our workers?

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for his excellent work on the Standing Committee on Immigration and Citizenship. I want to mention, in response to his excellent question, that developing our defence industrial base is absolutely critical to what we are trying to do and what this bill is trying to help us do in terms of strengthening Canada's defence sector.
We are aiming to have 70% of defence acquisitions go to Canadian firms and to create up to 125,000 good-paying jobs. I will tell colleagues how that is going to be good for—
Resuming debate, the hon. member for Saanich—Gulf Islands.
Mr. Speaker, I thank my hon. colleague from Davenport for splitting her time with me.

I am rising at this hour, grateful for the chance to address Bill C-40, but I am very much wanting to share with other members in this place that, as we are speaking here, there is a group of very dedicated peace activists making their way to Ottawa. They call themselves the peace train. I joined them on Friday in Vancouver and rode with them as far as I could before having to get off the train to make sure I got an airplane back to Ottawa in time for today's debate, but it is telling and important that people across Canada are increasingly being drawn to the peace movement. They recognize that our country is going through a transformation from being a country celebrated around the world for historic work for peace.

Of course, former prime minister Lester B. Pearson won the Nobel Peace Prize for creating peacekeepers within the United Nations. He did so when resolving the Suez crisis, which at the time cost the lives of Commonwealth soldiers, some of whom are still buried in Gaza. We cannot reach their graves, of course, because of the ongoing genocide, but we gathered on that peace train. Their slogan is, “Train is a verb”, and they are calling for the re-establishment of the Lester B. Pearson peacekeeping centre for training.

We are now falling behind allies around the world in our failure to keep up with the numbers and support for peacekeepers. I learned the other day that we have cut funding for the removal of landmines. One of our more recent signature accomplishments under the former minister for foreign affairs, the Hon. Lloyd Axworthy, was the Ottawa process that led to the treaty to ban landmines. We are MIA on the treaty for the prohibition of nuclear weapons. We do not even send observer delegations to the UN meetings, although some of us as parliamentarians do attend with global parliamentarians for the prohibition of nuclear war.
As such, it is worth noting this with great sadness.

I should mention we were greeted at the Edmonton train station by one of my heroes, the former member of parliament for Edmonton Strathcona. He served as a Progressive Conservative in that capacity, and then he was a senator in the Canadian Senate and the ambassador to the United Nations from Canada on nuclear disarmament, a position that no longer exists, which is telling all on its own. The hon. Doug Roche met us and encouraged us. He said to please take the message forward that Canada needs to be active in nuclear disarmament. We are not.

Right now and in this debate, there is no doubt. On behalf of the Green Party, I need to say that we support making sure that we address the gaps in adequate support to our military, the brave, very dedicated and self-sacrificing young men and women who choose to join the Canadian Armed Forces. Of course, very heavy on our hearts right now is the tragic loss in CFB Wainwright from the wildfire of last weekend, but it is worth noting that there is a transformation happening in Canadian society writ large, where, in referring to military spending, we no longer refer to it as something we need to do in our own defence, but as a growth sector for our economy.

It was not that long ago that former president Eisenhower warned the United States of the perils of relying on a military-industrial complex, but we are building one here. Our arms exports have gone up dramatically. We did not used to be an arms-trading country. Project Ploughshares tracked it and just reported last year that there was an all-time high of billions of dollars coming into Canada from our sale of military equipment and military arms, yet sometimes we dress this up as though we are supporting a Canadian defence sector.

I noted just before the last speech, and the member for Nanaimo—Ladysmith made note of the fact, that nothing in Bill C-40 says that where we spend money on defence has to benefit the Canadian economy, especially when we move more and more to arm's length. That spending could be supporting U.S. corporations, or whatever, around the world where armaments are made or jet fighters are built. We want to be spending money on those and will be doing so increasingly at arm's length from political accountability.

Of the newly announced spending since last year's budget from the government, fully 70% of new spending is going to the military. I will also highlight this announcement: The Prime Minister announced that a subsidy of $2 billion in federal public funds, described as building Canadian jobs and supporting Canadian industry, will be going to General Dynamics' operations in London, Ontario, to build armoured personnel vehicles. Of course, General Dynamics in London, Ontario, is a wholly owned subsidiary of General Dynamics in the United States, so there is nothing there about where we are putting our funding and building in preparation for our own defence, which Canadians certainly support.

There is a lot of concern over our defence in the Arctic, a vast region where we are inadequately prepared for conflict. We are very concerned as Greens about making sure that the Canadian navy has the resources it needs. We are an ocean nation with three oceans, and we are not even prepared for the kind of marine surveillance we need against illegal fishing. There are a lot of ways in which we need to see defence spending lifted.
Bill C-40 fits into a pattern that I am seeing from the new government, and I want to spend some time speaking of the pattern that extends beyond military spending.

Of course, as we know, the Defence Investment Agency was created on October 2 of last year as a special operating agency. Other members have mentioned what has gotten done since the creation of this special operating agency, and now we would be moving it to a Crown corporation. It is important to note that while the CBC website says that the Canadian corporation for defence investment “will report to a newly created associate minister of defence”, the bill does not say that. It says that the Governor in Council “may” create a position for an associate minister of defence. When it refers to the responsible minister, it does not say the responsible minister is the Minister of National Defence. It says that at some point in the future, cabinet would decide who the responsible minister for this bill should be. Meanwhile, decisions would be made increasingly by a Crown corporation that operates at arm's length from the government.

We know that when we have debates in this place, people ask things like whether the government will commit to restoring a line for VIA Rail, for example, which is a debate I remember from within the last day or so. The response from Liberal members is that they cannot interfere with a Crown corporation. They cannot tell it that it must restore a stop because it is a Crown corporation and is separate. This bill would indeed create a Crown corporation. The Defence Investment Agency would be a Crown corporation and would remove a level of direct accountability in a line of authority to the minister.

The other thing that happens is that sometimes my Conservative colleagues refer to this as the growth of bureaucracy, but I question that, because the people working in these Crown corporations do not necessarily work as civil servants within the Government of Canada. They can be hired from the private sector or wherever they come from.

I am drawn to a comparison, and this may seem far afield. There is a corporation called Epiq. The Government of Canada, through Health Canada, has given Epiq the contract to manage the class-action funds available for the thalidomiders, the people in Canada who have had a lifetime of experience as survivors of thalidomide. They do not like the term “victims”. Epiq, a foreign for-profit corporation, is making $1 million a year in often refusing basic justice to thalidomiders.

That is just a small piece of a growing pattern of passing things out of government over to third party private sector consultants. I question if Bill C-40 will deliver results for our defence contractors, our military and our men and women in uniform, or if it will be just another shadowy government operation that we cannot track.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I know that the leader of the Green Party, who has been around for many years, whether as a parliamentarian or a non-parliamentarian, is always looking at how governments can be made accountable. I am sure she is aware of this. We talk about Crown corporations. I believe that with a proper mission statement, a Crown corporation can do society a great favour being at arm's length from government. I am sure the member would agree with that. The issue is making sure that there is a transitional action to support transparency and accountability. I believe this legislation provides for that.
Does the member have some specific amendments she would like to bring forward? Even if she does not name them now, I think providing them to the minister would be advantageous.

Mr. Speaker, yes, I will bring forward amendments to committee, and I will certainly propose them to the minister. The difficulty is the pattern. We have seen it with Build Canada Homes, which was first a special operating agency with no accountability and then a Crown corporation. Now there is the Defence Investment Agency, which was first a special operating agency. I imagine that next we will see the Major Projects Office be made into a Crown corporation.

Again, there were two rounds of announcements and a flurry of setting things up that may or may not deliver results. Certainly, the legislation would not ensure anything. It has a lot of wide open space for future decisions.
Mr. Speaker, I am not necessarily opposed to a Crown corporation. There are many examples of Crown corporations that have worked well. There are examples of ones that have been quite the opposite.

What it says in the bill is that the Defence Investment Agency “must”, not “may”, follow the direction of the newly created associate minister. Does the member worry that this is putting too much power, in fact almost ultimate power, into the control of one person, who would be in control of billions of dollars? Does that cause her concern?

Mr. Speaker, that is a lot of power in the hands of one minister, but the legislation is like a pretzel. It does not say that there will be an associate minister of natural defence for procurement. It just says, in clause 13, that the Governor General “may” appoint an associate minister. It is possible to imagine that there will never be one.
Mr. Speaker, some people are in good shape. I congratulate the pages for their outstanding work.

Very briefly, I want to hear my colleague speak to any amendments that could be proposed. Personally, I am very concerned about accountability. When we asked, the procurement ombudsman said there is nothing he can do. If the ombudsman has absolutely no oversight authority, how can we put some kind of safeguard in place to ensure that everything stays above board?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Bloc Québécois's participation in committees is important. Unfortunately, I do not have the opportunity to sit on committees as a member. I will still present amendments because it is not just a matter of speed. It is a matter of accountability. I see that as the key issue.
Mr. Speaker, does the leader of the Green Party have the intention of supporting the legislation so that it goes to the committee stage?

Mr. Speaker, I certainly support it going to the committee stage, but I hope the government will not run roughshod over the committee and insist on inadequate testimony and witnesses. Too many committees are rushed to conclusion under the new government, and I find it very difficult to say that bills have been properly studied.

Mr. Speaker, when rising on a debate about defence procurement, the debate needs to start with an acknowledgement and a thanks to the people it is intended to serve. That is the men and women who serve in our Canadian Armed Forces and who have served in our Canadian Armed Forces. I think it is especially important as we approach Remembrance Day, but it is something we need to do every single day of the year. We need to remember, pay our respects to and show appreciation for what they have done for the freedoms that we all enjoy. I know there are a number of veterans here in the House, even at this present moment.

I want to point out that I am so honoured to live in the community of Airdrie, Alberta. It is so great at showing respect and remembrance. Just yesterday, I had the opportunity to join, as I do most years, in placing crosses at the LAV monument that we have for our Afghanistan mission and those who served in it at our museum in Airdrie. It was organized by the Airdrie Veterans Memorial Committee. People like Jason and Shawnee Hoffman, Bob McNevin, Dianne Kuhn and others were instrumental in making this happen. This gave us an opportunity to place a cross on the ground in front of the LAV monument for each of the 158 Canadian Armed Forces members who gave their lives serving our country in Afghanistan.

This weekend coming up, I will have an opportunity, on Veterans Boulevard, to lay crosses for all who have fallen in all the different conflicts we have served in, the local members of our community who have given their lives in sacrifice for our freedoms. It is such an honour to represent a community that gets that right. Of course, we will have our major Remembrance Day ceremony organized by the Airdrie legion branch. I just want to make sure that we all remember, when we are talking about defence procurement, that this is what it is all about. It is about the men and women who serve this country and we need to make sure that we get it right for them.

When standing to talk about Bill C-40, that is where the struggle is for me. It seems like the government's answer to everything is more government bureaucracy. That is what we are seeing in this bill. It is another example in a long list of examples. Conservatives clearly support getting the brave men and women of our Canadian Armed Forces the equipment they need to defend our country and to do their jobs. We support a process that is efficient, that is accountable and that is driven by operational requirements. What we struggle with and what we cannot support is treating another organizational chart as a substitute for actual procurement.

There is a record that is worth remembering. When our forces needed equipment for operations in Afghanistan, our previous Conservative government moved to ensure we acquired those essential capabilities. That included things like the Leopard 2 battle tanks, Chinook helicopters, Hercules tactical transport aircraft, C-17 Globemaster strategic airlifter, M777 howitzers and LAVS, armoured vehicles. All of those were among the equipment that was purchased during that period of time. They were not just announcements about a future process. They were the kinds of capabilities that our forces needed right then to do their jobs.

We also launched the national shipbuilding strategy and we ensured that Canadian businesses had opportunities in the F-35 production and supply chain. Our position has been that Canadian industry should benefit from defence investment, though the military must still be able to acquire proven equipment quickly when it cannot be produced here in time. However, the first consideration should always be the security of Canada and the operational needs of our men and women in the Canadian Armed Forces.

I think the F-35 is a particularly instructive example of what happens when political decisions keep changing the course of procurement. The Conservative government announced the F-35 as the intended replacement for the CF-18s. In 2015, of course, Justin Trudeau campaigned on a promise not to buy the F-35s. The Liberal government then pursued an interim Super Hornet option before launching another competition in 2017.

In 2022, after all of that, the Liberal government actually selected the F-35. Then in 2025, the government put procurement under review again. Canada is actually now contractually committed to 16 aircraft, while the fate of the remainder remains completely uncertain. Our pilots cannot defend Canadian airspace with another political reset. They need clarity about the aircraft that they will fly. They need the infrastructure that will support them and the timetable for bringing that capability into service. They need planes. They need jets. That is what they need.

That is a perfect example of the kinds of delays and bungling that we see from the Liberal government when it comes to defence procurement. This problem is not confined to fighter aircraft. There are also questions about the government's announcement that it had entered into negotiations with Saab concerning the GlobalEye airborne early warning and control platform. That was an announcement of a preferred supplier, not a signed procurement contract. Conservatives have called for the Auditor General and the Parliamentary Budget Officer to examine whether the appropriate process was followed, and whether the air force's operational requirements were properly considered.

Canadians deserve to know how these decisions are being made, whether the operational needs of the armed forces are being put first and whether taxpayers are getting the best possible value for their money. At the same time, the condition of the equipment already in service shows why decisions matter and why decisions need to happen quickly. The 2024-25 national defence figures show that 59.6% of key maritime fleets, 51% of key land fleets and 42.3% of key aerospace fleets are not serviceable. Our soldiers, sailors and aviators need working equipment. They do not need just simple announcements about how Ottawa will organize the procurement process. They actually need the equipment.

Now let us consider this so-called Defence Investment Agency. In October of last year, the Liberals established this Defence Investment Agency as a special operating agency within Public Services and Procurement Canada. In the spring of this year, they proposed a stand-alone agency through Bill C-31, and now, with Bill C-40, they propose a Crown corporation under a new associate minister of national defence for procurement. That is three versions of the same initiative in about a year. They are not even able to be efficient at creating efficiencies.

The government's own plans proposed about $31 million over four years to establish the original agency, and then another $104 million over five years to establish the stand-alone entity. However, the question still remains, what did the original structure actually deliver? What did the second proposal solve? Why are we now being asked to approve a third model before Canadians can have a clear accounting of results, if any? The Liberals promised to remove duplicative approvals and red tape when they created this agency, that was supposed to be the point of it. Yet here we are debating another structure, another board and another ministerial title. It is more bureaucracy. The government needs to tell Parliament and Canadians which decisions were delayed, which barriers remain and how this bill supposedly removes them. Otherwise, it risks replacing them with yet another announcement.

The bottom line here is the men and women in uniform serve this country and defend our freedoms, putting their lives on the line every day. Wainwright, of course, is a tragic example of how every single day they put on that uniform, their lives are on the line. What we as parliamentarians owe them and what the government owes them is to ensure they have the equipment and the resources they need to do their jobs. What we seem to be getting from the government, instead, is more bureaucracy, delays and red tape. The one thing that we never seem to see is actual results for the men and women who we send, on behalf of this country, to defend our freedoms, and that is pathetic.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, just because a Conservative says it, does not make it true. We have a record number of people applying to become members of the forces. In fact, last year was a 30-year high.

We have a Prime Minister and a government that is investing 2% of the GDP into the Canadian Forces. We can contrast that to the 1%. If we factor out the Coast Guard element being brought in, like the United States has done, we are still miles ahead of what the member's leader, when he sat in cabinet, had in contributions to the Canadian Forces.
The pay has gone up, as well as the materials, and now we are talking about a Crown corporation. Tell us why you oppose Crown corporations.
I will not be answering the question, and the parliamentary secretary knows he is not to speak directly to the member.
I will let the member for Airdrie—Cochrane respond.

Mr. Speaker, the first thing I notice from what the member had to say is that Liberals like to choose their words very carefully, because they have to keep their story straight. If they do not keep their story straight, then no one is going to believe them. The bottom line is that people do not believe what they have to say. When the member says that applications to join the Canadian Armed Forces are up, well, the problem is that there is another example where the Liberals' red tape and their bureaucracy gets in the way. It is such a slow process that many people end up dropping out of that process before they ever get through it. That is the first problem.

The second thing I will point out is that we hear time and time again from members who serve in our Canadian Armed Forces about the delays in getting their procurement. We have also heard from veterans who have served this country about getting the benefits they have earned through their service to this country, which is because there are too many bureaucratic processes already. All the Liberals are proposing to do is add more bureaucratic process on top of all that. That is not going to fix the problem.

Mr. Speaker, earlier in my speech, I mentioned the concern that an agency like this could become a place merely for rubber-stamping, where people just sign off and say, “There you go, it's done.” I would like to know whether my colleague shares this concern about a structure where parliamentarians may not always be aware of what is going on and cannot keep a close eye on things to make sure the Prime Minister's friends are not given preferential treatment.

Mr. Speaker, at the end of the day, what matters is delivering results. The members of the Canadian Armed Forces must be given the resources they need to do their jobs. There must be no additional bureaucracy. That is all that matters.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Bob Zimmer (Prince George—Peace River—Northern Rockies, CPC):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, first of all, I want to thank the member for his advocacy for veterans. I do not know anybody who has been stronger as an advocate for our vets over the last number of years.

This is what Liberals do with a bill like this. When they really do not want to do something, they say, “You know, we need a law in order to do the right thing”, when they could be doing the right thing as it is. When Liberals really want to do something, the Prime Minister just does it on his own. Whether he wants to be an EU associate member or have a gun grab, he just does it, but when the Liberals do not want to do something, they create a need for a bill.
Is another bill really necessary for another bureaucracy for the government to do the right thing when it comes to military procurement?

Mr. Speaker, the answer is simply no. The bottom line is that the men and women of the armed forces need the equipment to do their jobs. They do not need more bureaucracy. The bill proposes to create more bureaucracy, but it does not necessarily propose to get the men and women the equipment they need to do their jobs, and that is the problem with the bill.

Mr. Speaker, it has been a typical day in Ottawa. I started off this morning speaking about the Liberal tanker ban and how the Liberals are piling on red tape instead of solving the problem, and lo and behold, here we are at the end of the day talking about military procurement. It is the same theme. It is more Liberal red tape instead of trying to cut through red tape to get results.

We have heard some fine speeches, with some things I even agree with from government members who were talking about the importance of the military and so forth, but what is the substance of the bill they put before the House today? It is a third iteration of a defence agency. It would be more bureaucracy: a new Crown corporation with unprecedented powers to administer. It would reshuffle the bureaucratic structures, giving the Liberals a bit more power with less accountability and not delivering on the results that Canadians expect.

We are, of course, debating this bill and this issue at a time of intensifying conflict and challenge around the world. I believe we are in the midst of a new kind of cold war, with escalating conflict and competition between free democratic nations and authoritarian revisionist powers that would like to undermine freedom, democracy, human rights and the rule of law. This is the nature of the struggle and competition we face today. In the midst of that challenge, we need a Canada that is strong, that meets its NATO spending commitments, that does not just focus on dollars but on capabilities and results, and that is building partnerships with like-minded democracies to stand up to authoritarian revisionist powers and expand the space of human freedom by defending the freedom of our people here at home and by defending and advancing the space of freedom around the world. This requires a strong and principled Canada acting based on our values and building up our capabilities.

In the midst of this, unfortunately, the Prime Minister has emphasized a foreign policy that prioritizes a renewed pivot to engagement with the CCP, which is the only thing consistent about Liberal policy over the last few decades. The one thing the Liberals have not changed is that they will always look for any excuse to deepen relationships with the Government of China, often in ways that are not at all in Canada's interests.

The Prime Minister also speaks about middle-power partnerships. It is important for the House to note that when the Prime Minister speaks of middle powers, it is a description of size, not values. There are many different kinds of middle powers, some with which we have many common interests and values and others with which we do not. We on this side of the House prefer instead to emphasize the importance of seeking strong partnerships with like-minded nations where we share common values and objectives and where we can work together to advance our interests and values in a challenging world.

All of these things require strengthened Canadian capacity and capabilities, which is why we have been calling for more investments in our military since the beginning. I recall that in 2015, in the very first thrown speech of the government, it called for a leaner military. It was signalling even then a desire to reduce the capacity of our military. Conservatives pushed back then. We have pushed back consistently, calling for a strong Canada with stronger capabilities in our military capacity and in other areas so that we can defend our interests and values here at home and around the world.

The tension that has been caused between Canada and the U.S. because of the decisions of the American administration is unfortunate. In the midst of that dynamic, it is all the more important that we emphasize the strength of Canada and the defence of our values, and that we not allow Liberal politicians to use this as an excuse to pivot toward tightening relationships with authoritarian powers. We need strong relationships with democracies. We need more democratic partners around the world. We need to strengthen our collaboration with democratic partners everywhere and to do so on a foundation of strengthening our own capacity and capabilities.

This bill, unfortunately, is not about doing this. This bill is not about moving toward the kinds of real changes and results that we need to see. Rather, it is about a bureaucratic reorganization, with bureaucratic changes that do not deliver the results that our country needs and that are required at this time. As I said at the beginning, we have a government that wants to send signals and talk about its commitment on certain things, but that has involved putting forward legislation that piles on, moves or shifts red tape without delivering results.

Bill C-40 is not going to strengthen our ability to equip our military in these challenging times. We have been calling on the government for years to make the commitments that are required. That includes defending our own security, defending our country from foreign interference. It includes addressing the very real threats to this country that come in various forms, combatting foreign interference, not developing strategic partnerships with powers that are hostile to our interests and our values, but instead building up our capacity, defending our interests and defending our security. That is very much what we need to be doing right now. In these times and in all times, we need a strong Canada with those enhanced capabilities. That is what we stand for in the opposition, in believing there is a better way and we need a government that is focused on results.

I will say, in conclusion, the government will ultimately be judged by the results. It is not going to be judged by the words, by the number of bills, by the fact that again we have a third iteration of a new defence procurement in barely more than as many months. The government will be judged by whether or not it delivers in defending our security, in protecting our country from hostile actors, in building up our economy and in the various commitments that it has made. We will hold it accountable not for the words, but for the results that are delivered on defence and on every other file.

Mr. Speaker, I have deep respect for my colleague, even though we sometimes have differences of opinion in the Standing Committee on Human Resources, Skills and Social Development and the Status of Persons with Disabilities.

The question I have for my colleague is this: Does my colleague truly believe in diversifying our markets in order to strengthen our trade ties with other countries, our allies, to be specific? Does he believe in that?

Mr. Speaker, not only do I support diversifying our trade, but I worked as a staffer in the Stephen Harper government that led the way on this diversification. In 2006, when Conservatives took office, we had barely any engagements in terms of free trade outside of North America. After Stephen Harper's tenure in office, we had signed free trade agreements with nations representing over two-thirds of the world's GDP, with Asia-Pacific, as well as the European free trade area, the European Union and various individual countries. We made significant progress. The problem was that the Liberal government that followed did not follow those trade agreements with the kinds of infrastructure development and development of opportunities that would have allowed us to seize those opportunities.

We needed to build up the infrastructure capacity to really realize the potential of those trade agreements, but it is not correct at all that this idea of diversifying our trading arrangements is something new. It is an old idea championed by Conservatives and left on the shelf by Liberals for 11 years.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to hear from my colleague, who is known in this House for his strong sense of ethics and who often speaks out precisely on issues concerning the close ties that might exist, for example, between a prime minister and a friend he appoints. Curiously, we realize that this is exactly what is happening with this proposed agency. I would like to hear my colleague's thoughts on this.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for the kind words. Yes, I think ethics in government is very important, and I am concerned about the concentration of power associated with this bill, as well as the potential abuses that could occur of that power. I look forward to further study on these issues at committee, but I very much share the concerns raised by my colleague and hope this issue will get more airing when it is studied at committee.

Mr. Speaker, I want to build on that last question a little bit. This organization, this Crown corporation, if it comes into existence, is going to have the ability to literally be accountable for tens, if not hundreds, of billions of Canadian taxpayer dollars. I have concerns over the lack of parliamentary oversight with the way this legislation is currently drafted and how this minister and this CEO will be reporting back, if at all, because it seems to be lacking that within the legislation itself.
Does the hon. colleague share the same concerns about the lack of parliamentary oversight and accountability within the bill?

Mr. Speaker, yes, I do. I thank my colleague for raising this issue. The fundamental question in the debate on Bill C-40 is what the legislation would actually change. This is an opportunity for us to talk about various issues in military performance, military procurement and foreign policy more broadly, but the question in our vote is, “What would this bill actually change?” The effect of this bill is a concentration of power, a lack of accountability and a bureaucratic restructuring to some extent, but it is designed to mask a lack of results we have seen from the government on this and many other files.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to come back to job creation in Canada. Can my colleague send a message to our small and medium-sized enterprises that Bill C-40 will benefit them and help them create good jobs?

Mr. Speaker, I am very concerned about the state of jobs in this country. We have not heard the government address this, but we have the lowest workforce participation in this country in almost 30 years. I have big concerns. We have put forward a substantial jobs plan to address it, which I will be talking about a little more in the upcoming late show, so stay tuned.
Is the House ready for the question?
Some hon. members: Question.
The Deputy Speaker: The question is on the motion.

If a member participating in person wishes that the motion be carried or carried on division, or if a member of a recognized party participating in person wishes to request a recorded division, I would invite them to rise and indicate it to the Chair.
There have been discussions among all parties to have Bill C-40 pass on division.
I declare the motion carried on division. Accordingly, the bill stands referred to the Standing Committee on National Defence.
Content.ProceduralText: (Motion agreed to, bill read the second time and referred to a committee)

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I suspect that if you were to canvass the House, you would find unanimous consent to call it 6:43 p.m. so we can adjourn the House.
It is agreed?
Some hon. members: Agreed.

SubjectOfBusinessContent.ParaText: A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 38 deemed to have been moved.

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I am following up on questions I asked earlier about jobs.

We face an ongoing jobs crisis in this country, most notably underlined by the latest job numbers, which show a 29-year low in workforce participation. That is, a smaller percentage of Canadians are in the workforce today than at any time in the last 29 years. In the midst of that, we see continuing hints by the government that it intends to increase payroll taxes, to increase the tax on jobs, and my earlier question was about whether the government intends to do that and why it is teasing the possibility of increasing the tax on jobs.
Conservatives are opposed to increasing the tax on jobs. We think this is the worst kind of tax, and certainly during a jobs crisis, increasing the tax on jobs is a terrible idea.

Meanwhile, my question highlighted the fact that the government is attacking vocational institutions by arbitrarily cutting off student grants to students at vocational institutions. This is notable because last week in the House, the minister responsible for jobs launched an absolutely vicious attack on career colleges on the floor of the House of Commons. It was really a shameful display from a minister of the Crown showing complete ignorance of the important role that vocational career colleges play in this country. It is shameful that the minister who is supposed to be responsible for jobs would say the things she said.

Here is what has happened. A few bad actors, in many respects masquerading as career colleges, have been allowed under the government to abuse the system and take advantage of immigration programs. There have been bad actors who have abused the system, and there has been a failure of enforcement in that regard. However, in response to that, the government has tried to tar all career colleges with the same brush, ignoring the fact that many career colleges do excellent work, are well regulated and provide critically important career-relevant training programs to Canadian students to prepare them for Canadian jobs.

We recognize on this side of the House that union training halls, not-for-profit colleges, universities and private vocational colleges are all part of an important training ecosystem that is working to prepare Canadian young people for Canadian jobs. The government's decision to arbitrarily cut off students who are learning career-relevant skills at private vocational institutions is not right and not defensible.

It has been hard for us up to now to understand why the government is doing this, but the ignorant and vicious attack on career colleges from the Minister of Jobs and Families that we heard last week in the House underlines exactly why we have this problem. It is because the minister has refused to engage with career colleges, refused to talk to students who are at those institutions and refused to understand the work they are doing.

The minister and the government should be ashamed of themselves. At a time when we desperately need trades workers, when we desperately need the right training that aligns with the needs of the labour market, and when vocational institutions are very much engaged with private sector companies to prepare young people for the jobs that exist in this country, we have a government that is arbitrarily cutting off students at career colleges. This is going to have a negative effect on young people, especially from middle- and low-income backgrounds, who are trying to get relevant labour market skills.
I want to ask the government if it will apologize for the outrageous display from the minister, ask her to rescind those comments and educate her about the issue.

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, if anyone should be apologizing, it would be the member across the way. I had to listen through four minutes of the member saying something that is, to be kind, a stretch of one's imagination in terms of reality, if I can put it that way.

If I were to tag onto his ending comments, one of the things I would highlight that came out of the spring economic budget for all Canadians was the investment and the commitment the Prime Minister and the government have made to a fantastic program, which is the Red Seal program. Members can think of the dozens of trades, skilled trades, that are out there. We have a government that is going to increase the numbers to somewhere between 80,000 to 100,000 Canadians. A vast majority, I would suggest to members, are young Canadians. Where do we think they are going to get the skills from? They are going to get the skills from the workforce and post-secondary institutions.

When we think of the reality of numbers and of recognizing the importance of our post-secondary institutions and, I must say, many of our secondary facilities across Canada, I think it is a very powerful statement of reality that the government has made the commitment to.

The member opposite makes reference to young people on the issue of jobs. Of course jobs are important. There is no doubt about that. As a government, since we were elected back in the last federal election, just over a year ago, we have had a net increase of jobs, at 150,000 plus. That is even at a time when we have had to deal with Trump tariffs in trade. We have still been able to get a net increase of 150,000-plus jobs. That does not mean we have stopped there. We continue to build that stronger and healthier economy by a number of initiatives that the government has brought forward, because we understand the value of jobs.

The member talks about youth unemployment. The member opposite was working for Stephen Harper when his leader was a part of the cabinet of Stephen Harper and when youth unemployment, back in 2012, averaged over 14% that year. Contrast that to the last year, where it is under 14%. Unlike the Conservatives back then, who actually cut things like summer youth programs, we continue to maintain them and, at the end of the day, look at expanding programs like our Red Seal program, which is going to get more youth working.

Of course we are concerned about youth unemployment. I believe that the government's actions have shown that. Of course we are concerned about overall unemployment. What does the member think is one of the driving factors for our Prime Minister, the cabinet and, in fact, the entire government caucus in pushing to build major projects? This attracted literally a half a trillion dollars of potential investments back in September when the Prime Minister hosted a summit for the world to come and talk about investing in Canada, which is historic amounts of money. This is not to mention the amounts of projects there are, working in collaboration with provinces and indigenous people, to build a stronger and healthier Canada for all.

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has a difficult job. He has to defend whatever nonsense lines of the government of the day. Here are the facts from Statistics Canada. In terms of job numbers, we are at a 29-year low in labour force participation. We can check the Statistics Canada job numbers to confirm that. A big part of the solution to that would be to train Canadian young people to fill Canadian jobs and to pursue strong alignment between what businesses are actually looking for in skills and what is being made available to young people in skills development, to train young Canadian people for Canadian jobs.

Rather than support vocational institutions that are at the front lines of doing this, the government made the arbitrary decision to cut off student grants to those students and then the minister viciously attacked those institutions on the floor of the House.

Right now, under the government, a Canadian student can get a grant to study in a foreign institution. They cannot get that grant to study those labour market skills at a career college right here in Canada. How does that make any sense?

Mr. Speaker, it is not defending the federal government; it is stating the facts of reality. The member might want to twist the numbers, but I used a very specific example. He was working for Stephen Harper in 2012, when the economy was doing well and youth unemployment was over 14%. Contrast that to under 14% with the current Prime Minister, given the environment we are in today.

Every job is important. We continue to push for more jobs for all ages. In terms of colleges and universities, how we train people, it is about working in collaboration with provinces. The provinces play a leading role in ensuring that the labour market is actually connecting post-secondary facilities with future employment opportunities. The federal government supports, co-operates with and works toward that.

Mr. Speaker, I am rising to follow up on a question I asked the Minister of National Defence about the now infamous Maritime Launch Services' so-called spaceport in Nova Scotia. Clearly this is a project where federal money is being spent, and has been spent, without proper due diligence. It is, of course, also being spent very quickly. Just to recap, it was $200 million over 10 years for a piece of property that the company is paying only $13,500 a year to lease. That is a great ROI for the company, but it is not so good for the Canadian taxpayer.

One area of concern I want to follow up on is the technology safeguards agreement. I see my colleague looking a little puzzled, so I will give him the opportunity to google it while I am asking my question. The technology safeguards agreement is a great idea. It is a government-to-government agreement that sets out the rules for protecting sensitive U.S.-origin space technology and technology that is used outside the U.S.

This is important, because without a technology safeguards agreement, U.S.-origin rockets or U.S.-origin technology cannot be launched from Canada, including from the concrete pad of Maritime Launch Services. Other countries have reached technology safeguards agreements with the United States, including, fairly recently, the United Kingdom. As I understand it, substantive negotiations were completed by Canada and the United States in August 2024, at least according to Global Affairs Canada press releases.

Could my colleague give the House an update on the status of that agreement, because it is completed but not yet signed and in force? Without that agreement, the company, which the government is now funding to the tune of $200 million, will be unable to launch any U.S.-origin technology or goods, which is the majority of the market it is seeking to access with its spaceport. Could my colleague give us an update on the government's status in getting this agreement completed?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, I was provided the question that was posed, and that is what tonight is supposed to be about: reflection on the question that was posed. The question the member posed the other day in the House was all about the spaceport and why the government is investing in a spaceport.

Unlike the Conservative Party, we recognize that the spaceport is not optional. It is mandatory. When the Prime Minister or the government talks about sovereignty, having the ability to launch is part of that. Canada is in a great position to work with the European Union and others in being able to launch satellites or other objects into space. This is critical, the ability not only to launch but to expand the industry here in Canada. We are talking about the potential of literally hundreds of millions or billions of dollars of future investments, developing an industry that is there already and advancing it significantly.

I think of Magellan in Winnipeg, which manufactures and produces satellites. We cannot put those into orbit. Canada does not have the ability today to launch military satellites, if doing so was deemed to be in our interest. We would have to approach other nations. We are creating a launch pad, and now we are also adding onto it one that, I believe, is in Newfoundland. The member might want to do a quick Google search on that. He will find that from a military perspective and, in particular the one we are talking about tonight, from a civilian perspective and in light of potential contracts, both internally and coming into Canada from other nations, it is in Canadians' best interest.

It is going to develop that industry so companies like Magellan and others in our nation will be able to advance in that whole spectrum of development and manufacturing. It will allow Canada to set its priorities. We will not have to go to SpaceX or any other foreign entity in order to do the things we believe are important as a nation. Also, this is a growing industry worldwide. Why would we not want to take advantage of the technology we have already and advance it to the next level?

Space sovereignty is very important. It is a part of the government's agenda. We will continue to move in that direction because it will give us not only sovereignty but the advancement of technology and growth of our workforce by providing good-quality jobs.

I would invite my colleague across the way to come to Winnipeg, visit Magellan and look at some of the things we can develop and have the potential to put into space. Some are already going into space, but that cannot be done from Canada. We have to go to other nations to get that done. I believe having the space launching pad will be a positive thing for all of us.

Mr. Speaker, I am not really debating the member on the potential benefits of having a space industry. That is not really the question. The question goes to the heart of what he suggests is the potential opportunity, because that opportunity, or at least a large portion of that opportunity, will not exist unless we complete this technology safeguards agreement.

I would invite him to ask Magellan whether it does anything that does not include U.S. technology. I would hazard to say that it does use U.S. technology, and it cannot be launched by rocketry in Canada if it uses U.S. technology. To access the opportunity, we need to complete this agreement. The reality is that many U.S. companies are further advanced than Canada when it comes to this. That is why a lot of rockets and things are being launched from the U.S. rather than Canada. If we want to do it ourselves, we have to build that expertise and knowledge here in Canada.
If the member does not know the answer, could he commit to coming back with an answer, or could he give us an update today? When will we see this agreement completed?

Mr. Speaker, that is a question the member might want to pose during question period. This is a follow-up to questions that are posed in question period for additional details. If the member is unable to get the answer, he can come back to me and I would be happy to see what I can do for him.

However, I want to sincerely invite the member to Magellan in Winnipeg. I think he might be surprised by the degree to which we have the technology already in Canada. In fact, I would argue that there are certain space element projects that the United States comes to Canada for. It is not just the United States. We have a labour force that not only can sustain itself on space development, but can grow that industry, and part of growing that industry is looking at having the ability to launch.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to follow up on a question I posed regarding the ethical cloud surrounding the Prime Minister in respect of decisions that his government has made to the benefit of Brookfield and, by extension, his personal financial portfolio.

It is an undisputed fact that the Prime Minister has vast conflicts of interest with respect to Brookfield. Indeed, he has acknowledged more than 100 such conflicts of interest. Notwithstanding this, he has dismissed concerns about these conflicts on the basis that his assets are in a blind trust. The problem with that, of course, is that his blind trust is not truly blind because he knows exactly what went into it.
Let us look at some of the facts.

The Prime Minister stands to make tens of millions of dollars in future bonus pay from a Brookfield investment fund that he set up when he was the chair of Brookfield. Accordingly, he knows exactly what companies the fund has invested in because he hand-picked the companies. What exactly is blind about that? Then there are the Brookfield stock options for which the Prime Minister stands to make millions. What is blind about that? All of this to say that there is nothing blind about his so-called blind trust.
Since the Prime Minister took office, time and again we have seen Brookfield at the front of the line, doing very well under the government. I will provide some examples.

The government funnelled half a billion dollars to the European Space Agency. Why the European Space Agency? Could it be because Brookfield has a 50% ownership in the space agency's headquarters? Could that be the reason or part of the reason?

Then, there is the Pathways Alliance carbon capture scheme, involving billions of dollars of investment in carbon capture. The leading carbon capture company connected to Pathways Alliance is Entropy. Who owns Entropy? None other than the same Brookfield investment fund the Prime Minister's future bonus pay is directly tied to. What a coincidence.
Then there is the $50-billion maple fund that ties the retirement savings of millions of Canadians to Brookfield, and on it goes.

Billions of dollars are flowing to Brookfield as a result of decisions made by the government. When Brookfield does well, the Prime Minister does well. That is verified by none other than the chief operating officer of Brookfield. What we have amounts to one big conflict of interest involving the Prime Minister.
In the face of that, the ethics committee issued a report in the spring calling on the Prime Minister to end these conflicts of interest by divesting himself fully from Brookfield. Why has he not?

Intervention.PersonSpeaking: Hon. Kevin Lamoureux (Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons, Lib.):

Content.ParaText: Mr. Speaker, what the member clearly demonstrates is that the Conservatives are more focused on personal attacks and character assassinations than they are on public policy and the many things this government has done.

I remember sitting in the third party in the House of Commons. When Justin Trudeau was first elected as leader of the Liberal Party, the Conservatives started personal attacks against him, and from day one after he became prime minister, consistently that is all they did. It is somewhat sad, because at the end of the day, it is this thing here, that thing there and this thing here, and then they line it all up, and oh my God we have a conspiracy. We call that a tin-hat theory.

The Prime Minister was the the governor of the Bank of Canada and the governor of the Bank of England, and he was an economist extraordinaire. He is very well respected around the world. Through his leadership, the government has made numerous decisions to build a stronger and healthier Canadian economy.

What we just saw is something we saw a bit earlier, when Conservative members stood up and said that the Crown corporation on military procurement is all about corruption. That is what some of them tried to imply, but it is good public policy. The Conservatives can continue to try to do character assassinations and try to paint everything as being corrupt. They can do that all they want, but at the end of the day, I can assure the member that our Prime Minister, who was elected just over a year ago, and this government are going to continue to be focused on Canadians and not the Conservative agenda.

If I were to put on a conspiracy hat, I could ask members to imagine all the Conservatives, when they were in government, voting for farm protection procedures or enhancements, or those who argue here for getting discounts on diesel. I could say they are trying to fill the pockets of their families and so forth because they are farmers: How can a person be a farmer and vote for something that is going to benefit a farmer? I do not do that. I do not question their integrity. I do not question the ethics of that, because we have an Ethics Commissioner. I have more faith in the Ethics Commissioner than I do in what I have witnessed from the official opposition over the last number of years, because its sole focus far too often seems to be on character assassination. I do not hear other entities outside of the House of Commons, such as NDP governments, Conservative governments, different stakeholders, and indigenous community leaders, talking about corruption in Ottawa.

Sure, there is always going to be room for improvement when working collaboratively, but I believe that as a government, we have been reaching out and working collaboratively with all levels of government in numerous areas. We will continue to do so because it is the right thing to do. It builds a stronger and healthier Canada for all.

Mr. Speaker, let me spell it out for the parliamentary secretary. The Prime Minister has significant financial interests in Brookfield. He elected not to divest himself of those interests. Consequently, he does well when Brookfield does well, and Brookfield has done very well under his government, to the tune of billions of dollars. Which of those facts does the parliamentary secretary dispute?

In addition to the so-called blind trust, which is not a blind trust, the Prime Minister set up an ethics screen, which he has repeatedly defied, including by meeting with Brookfield on multiple occasions in direct contravention of the screen the Ethics Commissioner set up. Also, he refuses to disclose times when conflicts were identified but he made a decision anyway. Why is the Prime Minister hiding those potential conflicts?

Mr. Speaker, as members know, the system we operate under today, in terms of blind trust and what the expectations are for prime ministers, is something that was in place long ago. In fact, I believe it was Stephen Harper who put it in place. The same rules have applied to Stephen Harper, to Justin Trudeau and to our current Prime Minister.

Our current Prime Minister has gone out of his way in working with the independent officers of the House of Commons, either directly or indirectly, to ensure that there is integrity in the system, including blind trust. I think it would have been the same for Prime Minister Stephen Harper.
